title: Authentication, authorization, web security
blurb: Sessions vs JWT, password hashing, XSS, CSRF, secrets. Every CRUD app has a login, and getting it wrong is the most consequential mistake a junior can ship.

questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
choices: Authentication is for human users; authorization is for service accounts
Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do
Authorization runs first, deciding who is allowed to attempt a login at all
They are two names for the same login check, used by different frameworks
questions.why: A logged-in user reading someone else's invoice is an authorization failure, not an authentication one, and it is the most common serious vulnerability in CRUD apps. Authentication happens first; authorization then runs on every request.
questions.asked: Universal. The strong answer gives an example of each failing separately.

questions.q: Why hash passwords with bcrypt or Argon2 rather than SHA-256?
choices: SHA-256 has been broken, so its hashes can be reversed back to the original password
They encrypt the password with a key, so it can be recovered for users
They produce longer output, so no two passwords can share the same hash
They are deliberately slow and salted, while SHA-256 is built to be fast
questions.why: A GPU computes billions of SHA-256 hashes per second. bcrypt's work factor makes each guess cost milliseconds, and the per-password salt defeats precomputed tables. Argon2id is also memory-hard, which blunts GPUs further. SHA-256 is not broken; it is simply the wrong tool.
questions.asked: Guaranteed if the role touches auth. "Salted and slow" covers it.

questions.q: Sessions or JWTs: what is the real trade-off?
choices: JWTs are more secure, because the signature stops anyone reading the claims
Sessions cannot work with mobile apps, since native clients never store cookies at all
Sessions are revocable but need shared state; JWTs are stateless but hard to revoke
JWTs are encrypted by the server, while session ids travel in plain text
questions.why: "Log out everywhere" and "ban this user now" are hard with a stateless token: you end up with a revocation list, which is server state again. The usual compromise is short-lived access tokens plus a revocable refresh token. Native apps can store cookies or session ids perfectly well.
questions.asked: A favourite because many candidates believe JWT is simply the modern, better option.

questions.q: Is the payload of a typical signed JWT encrypted?
choices: Yes: the server encrypts it with its secret, so only the server can read it
Only the claims are encrypted; the header stays readable for routing
Yes, once sent over HTTPS, so whoever holds the token cannot read it
No: it is base64url-encoded and readable; the signature only proves integrity
questions.why: Anyone can paste a JWT into a decoder and read the claims, so never put anything sensitive in them. The signature proves who issued it and that it was not altered. Encrypted JWTs (JWE) exist but are rare; TLS protects the token in transit, not from whoever holds it.
questions.asked: A quick, decisive filter question.

questions.q: What is XSS, and what actually stops it?
choices: Script injected into your page; stopped by capping the length of every input
Script injected into your page; stopped by serving every page of the site over HTTPS
Script injected into your page; stopped by contextual output encoding plus CSP
Script injected into your page; stopped by hashing user input before saving
questions.why: Encode on output, in the right context (HTML body, attribute, URL and JavaScript each differ). React escapes interpolated values by default; `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` is the opt-out. A Content-Security-Policy limits the damage when something slips through. Short payloads like `<script src=//x.io>` pass any length cap.
questions.asked: Checks you know the fix is on output, not input, which is the common misconception.

questions.q: What is CSRF, and why does it work?
choices: An attacker steals the session cookie by reading document.cookie in a script
An attacker injects script into your page that submits forms on your behalf
Another site triggers a request, and the browser attaches your cookies to it
An attacker guesses a valid session id by trying sequential values quickly
questions.why: The attacker never sees the response; they only need the side effect. Defences: SameSite=Lax or Strict cookies, an anti-forgery token, and checking Origin. Bearer tokens in a header are not vulnerable, because the browser does not attach them automatically. Injected script on your own page is XSS, which defeats CSRF defences.
questions.asked: Checks you can explain the mechanism (ambient cookies), which is what makes the defences make sense.

questions.q: In a browser app, which token storage is safest against theft by injected script?
choices: localStorage, since only scripts from your own origin are able to read it
sessionStorage, since it is cleared when the tab closes and cannot leak
An HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, which page scripts cannot read
A variable inside a JavaScript module, which other scripts cannot reach
questions.why: HttpOnly keeps the token out of reach of any script, while Web Storage is readable by every script on your origin, injected ones included. Injected code can still patch `fetch` to capture an in-memory token. Cookies bring CSRF back, so pair them with SameSite and an anti-forgery token.
questions.asked: The criterion is in the stem; the follow-up is what an attacker can still do with XSS even when the token is HttpOnly.

questions.q: Why should a login form return the same error for 'wrong password' and 'no such user'?
choices: One message is simpler to translate and keep consistent across the UI
Checking the user first needs an extra database query on each login
Data-protection law forbids telling users their password is wrong
Different messages let an attacker find out which accounts exist
questions.why: Timing can leak it too: run the password hash even when the user does not exist, so both paths take the same time. The same reasoning applies to password reset and signup forms.
questions.asked: The timing follow-up separates people who have thought about it from people who memorised the rule.

questions.q: What does least privilege mean for the database account your app uses?
choices: Only administrators may connect directly; the app has to go through them
It gets only what it needs: no DROP or schema changes in production
Each environment uses its own password, rotated every quarter
The connection string is encrypted, so a leak reveals nothing
questions.why: It limits the blast radius of an injection or a leaked credential. Migrations run under a separate, more privileged account in the pipeline, not the runtime one. Rotating or encrypting the credential is good hygiene but does not reduce what it can do once stolen.
questions.asked: Checks you design for the day a control fails.

questions.q: How should secrets reach a production app?
choices: From appsettings.Production.json, committed next to the code that uses it
From a .env file committed to the repo for the whole team's convenience
Hard-coded in the source but obfuscated so scanners cannot find them
From a secret manager or injected environment variables, never the repo
questions.why: Git history is forever; deleting a committed secret does not remove it, so a leaked one must be rotated. Locally, use user secrets or an uncommitted .env with a committed .env.example.
questions.asked: The follow-up is "a secret was committed; what now?" Rotate it.

questions.q: What does a refresh token do?
choices: It extends the current access token's expiry each time the user is active
It gets a new short-lived access token without a new login, and can be revoked
It re-signs the session cookie so that the browser keeps it for another full period
It rotates the server's signing key so older access tokens stop working
questions.why: Access tokens stay short-lived (minutes), so revocation matters less, while the refresh token, stored more carefully and revocable server-side, carries the long-lived trust. Rotate refresh tokens on each use so a stolen one is detected when it is replayed. Tokens cannot be extended; a new one is issued.
questions.asked: Checks you know why two tokens exist rather than one long-lived one.

questions.q: What is broken object-level authorization (BOLA)?
choices: Missing role checks on admin endpoints, so any user can call admin actions
Using sequential ids, which let attackers guess the next record in a table
Checking the user is logged in but not that the requested record is theirs
Failing to expire sessions, so a stolen token keeps working indefinitely
questions.why: `GET /orders/1234` returns someone else's order because the query filtered by id but not by owner. It is the top API vulnerability, and it is invisible in tests written by the person who wrote the bug. Missing admin checks are function-level authorization; guessable ids only make BOLA easier to exploit.
questions.asked: If you can name this and say how you would prevent it, you are ahead of most candidates.

questions.q: What is OAuth 2.0 actually for?
choices: Authenticating users by proving their identity to your application directly
Delegated authorization: an app acts for you at a service, without your password
Encrypting API traffic between services, as an extra layer on top of TLS
Single sign-on between your own services, by sharing one session cookie
questions.why: OAuth issues access tokens that let a client call an API on a user's behalf. OpenID Connect is the authentication layer built on top of it; "Sign in with Google" is OIDC. Using a raw OAuth access token as proof of login is a classic misuse.
questions.asked: Checks you know the OAuth/OIDC split that every "Sign in with..." button depends on.

questions.q: Why does 'we validate on the client' not secure an API?
choices: Client-side validation code is often buggy, so it misses some bad inputs
It slows the page, so users switch off JavaScript and skip the checks
It does secure it, provided the client is a compiled mobile app
Anyone can call the API directly with curl; the client is not trusted
questions.why: Client validation exists for UX: fast feedback. Every rule that matters must be enforced on the server, because the server is the only place you control. A compiled app can be decompiled, or bypassed entirely with a proxy.
questions.asked: A junior filter: the trust boundary is the whole point.

questions.q: What does `SameSite=Strict` do to this cookie?
choices: It is only sent to the exact subdomain that set it, never to the parent
It is only ever sent over HTTPS connections, never over plain HTTP
It is never sent on cross-site requests, even when following a link in
It is hidden from JavaScript, so document.cookie cannot read its value
questions.why: Strict breaks "click the link in the email and arrive logged in", because that navigation starts on another site. Lax allows top-level GET navigations, which is why it is the sensible default for session cookies. HTTPS-only is `Secure` and script-hiding is `HttpOnly`.
questions.asked: Checks you know each cookie attribute does one job, and the UX cost of Strict.

questions.q: What does rate limiting a login endpoint protect against?
choices: Distributed denial of service, which it blocks entirely at the edge
Credential stuffing and brute force, limited per account and per IP
SQL injection, since each attacker gets fewer tries at a payload
Session hijacking, since stolen cookies can only be replayed so often
questions.why: Limit per account too, not only per IP: a distributed attack uses thousands of IPs against one account. Pair it with breached-password checks and MFA. A login limit does nothing for injection, which parameterised queries fix.
questions.asked: The per-account follow-up is what distinguishes a considered answer.

questions.q: From a security standpoint, why build SQL with parameters even after escaping quotes in user input?
choices: Concatenated SQL runs more slowly, because the database cannot reuse its plan
Modern databases refuse concatenated queries unless a legacy flag is set
Escaping has encoding and context edge cases; parameters keep data out of the SQL
Escaping corrupts names such as O'Brien, which then fail to save
questions.why: Parameters are sent separately from the query text, so they can never become SQL keywords. Plan reuse is a real bonus but not a security property. The one place you still need care is dynamic identifiers: an ORDER BY column cannot be a parameter, so it must come from an allow-list.
questions.asked: The dynamic ORDER BY follow-up checks you know where parameters stop helping.

questions.q: TLS terminates at your load balancer, which forwards plain HTTP to the app servers. What is still unencrypted?
choices: Nothing: TLS keeps the payload encrypted end to end until the app reads it
Only the headers; the load balancer re-encrypts every body it forwards
Only the URL path; cookies and Authorization headers stay encrypted
Traffic from the balancer to the apps, headers and bodies included
questions.why: Termination means the balancer decrypts; everything after it, passwords and bearer tokens included, crosses the internal network in clear. That is often accepted inside a private network, but compliance or zero-trust setups re-encrypt to the backend.
questions.asked: Checks you know where your TLS actually ends, which matters for audits and for what an internal attacker can see.

questions.q: What is a Content-Security-Policy?
choices: A written policy the security team keeps on how content gets reviewed
A CORS setting listing the origins that may call your API from a browser
A response header limiting where scripts, styles and more may load from
A cookie attribute that stops page scripts reading or changing a cookie
questions.why: It is defence in depth for XSS: even if a script is injected, a strict CSP means the browser refuses to run it. Rolling one out usually means removing inline scripts first, which is the hard part. CORS controls who can read your API's responses, a different problem.
questions.asked: Checks you know CSP by its mechanism and can name why it is hard to adopt.

questions.q: A user changes their password. What should happen to their existing sessions?
choices: Nothing: sessions are independent of the password once they exist
End all other sessions, since a change often follows a compromise
End only the current session, so the user signs in again right here
End only sessions older than 30 days, since recent ones are trusted
questions.why: With server-side sessions this is a delete; with stateless JWTs you need a per-user token version or a revocation list, the practical cost of statelessness. Ending the current session as well is also acceptable; keeping an attacker's session alive is not.
questions.asked: A good scenario question because it forces the candidate back to the session/JWT trade-off.

questions.q: What is the risk of returning detailed error messages from an API?
choices: They make responses larger, which slows clients on poor networks
They break JSON parsing in clients that expect one fixed error shape
Stack traces and SQL errors reveal internals that help an attacker
None, once the endpoint requires authentication to be called
questions.why: Log the detail with a correlation id and return a generic message with that id to the client. Support can then find the full error without exposing it. Authenticated users can be attackers too.
questions.asked: Leads to the correlation-id pattern, which is the practical answer.

questions.q: How should a team handle vulnerabilities reported in its dependencies?
choices: Ignore advisories until one is actually exploited against the service
Pin every dependency forever, so that no new vulnerability can arrive
Audit in CI, patch on a schedule, and check the path is reachable
Upgrade everything to latest the moment any advisory is published
questions.why: Run `npm audit` or `dotnet list package --vulnerable` in the pipeline. Not every advisory is exploitable in your usage, but "we never looked" is not defensible. Pinning forever freezes known vulnerabilities in place; blind upgrades ship breaking changes.
questions.asked: Checks for a sustainable process rather than panic or neglect.

questions.q: Why should uploads not be stored under the web root with the user's filename?
choices: A filename can traverse directories or carry an extension the server runs
A long filename can exceed the filesystem limit and crash the upload
Files under the web root use up disk faster than an object store would
The CDN cannot cache files whose names contain spaces or Unicode
questions.why: Generate your own identifier, keep the original name as metadata only, check the content by inspecting the file rather than trusting the header, and serve from a separate origin or object store. A `.php` or `.aspx` file under the web root may be executed.
questions.asked: Checks you treat every part of an upload, name included, as attacker-controlled.

questions.q: What is defence in depth?
choices: Encrypting sensitive data several times over with different keys and algorithms
Having a dedicated security team review every change before it merges
Running a yearly penetration test and fixing whatever it reports
Layering independent controls so that one failure does not expose the system
questions.why: Parameterised queries and least-privilege database accounts and input validation and monitoring. Any single control eventually fails; the question is what catches it when it does.
questions.asked: Checks you think in layers; the strong answer names two concrete layers for one threat.

questions.q: How does an authenticator app's six-digit code (TOTP) work as a second factor?
choices: The server texts it to the phone each time the user starts a login
It is derived from a secret shared at enrolment and the current time
It is a hash of the password, recomputed by the app every 30 seconds
The server generates it and pushes it to the app over a secure channel
questions.why: At enrolment (the QR code) the app and server share a secret; both compute HMAC(secret, current 30-second window), so the app works offline and proves possession of the device. SMS codes are weaker (SIM swap). TOTP can still be phished in real time, which passkeys prevent.
questions.asked: Checks you know MFA beyond "a code on your phone", including where it falls short.

questions.q: Which design for password reset tokens is safest?
choices: A JWT holding the user id, valid for a week so slow users can finish
The user id encrypted with the app key, so no database row is needed
A random token stored in plain text, valid until the next login
Random, single-use, expiring within an hour, stored only as a hash
questions.why: A reset token is a temporary password, so treat it like one: unguessable, short-lived, invalidated on use, and hashed so a database leak does not hand out working links. A self-contained token cannot be made single-use without server state anyway.
questions.asked: Every app has a reset flow; checks you apply password thinking to it.

questions.q: Using express-session, what is the security flaw in this login handler?
choices: The session id is not regenerated on login, so a planted id gets logged in
Storing userId in the session lets the user edit it from the browser
Redirecting after the POST leaks the password in the Referer header
Returning 401 on a bad password lets an attacker enumerate accounts
questions.why: Session fixation: an attacker who planted a known session id in the victim's browser shares the session once the victim logs in. Call `req.session.regenerate()` before setting `userId`. Session data lives on the server, and both failure paths here return the same 401.
questions.asked: A code-review question that checks you know login must change the session id, not just add to it.

questions.q: In OpenID Connect, how do the ID token and the access token differ?
choices: The ID token is sent to APIs as proof; the access token is only shown in the UI
They are the same JWT, issued twice so one copy can be refreshed later on
The ID token is encrypted for the user; the access token is plain JSON
The ID token tells your client who signed in; the access token goes to APIs
questions.why: The ID token's audience is your client app: it describes the login (who, when, how). The access token's audience is the resource server, and it may be opaque to the client. Sending ID tokens to your API as bearer tokens is a common misuse.
questions.asked: Checks you have integrated a real identity provider rather than copied a tutorial.

questions.q: Why must a single-page or mobile app use PKCE with the authorization code flow?
choices: PKCE encrypts the access token so that browser extensions cannot read it
PKCE replaces the redirect, so tokens never pass through the browser at all
It cannot keep a client secret, so PKCE proves the code goes to its requester
PKCE lets the app skip the login page when the user already has a session
questions.why: The app sends a hash of a random verifier with the authorization request and the verifier itself when redeeming the code, so an intercepted code is useless to anyone else. A secret shipped in a public client is not secret. OAuth 2.1 makes PKCE mandatory for every client, and the implicit flow is deprecated.
questions.asked: The standard modern answer to "how does your SPA log in?"; the implicit flow is the outdated one.

questions.q: An attacker loads your 'Delete account' page in an invisible iframe over a decoy button. Which response header stops it?
choices: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' (or X-Frame-Options)
Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to your origin, which forbids framing
Strict-Transport-Security, so the page only ever loads over HTTPS
Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, so the framing page cannot see the URL
questions.why: Clickjacking relies on your page rendering inside theirs. `frame-ancestors` (the modern form of `X-Frame-Options: DENY`) makes the browser refuse to render it in a frame. CORS governs reading responses with fetch, not embedding pages.
questions.asked: Checks you know which header solves which browser attack.

questions.q: After login this handler redirects to `?next=`. What does an attacker gain from `?next=https://evil.example`?
choices: The session cookie, which the browser sends on to the redirect target
Code execution, because res.redirect evaluates the URL as a script
A phishing link on your real domain that lands victims on their site
Nothing, because browsers block redirects to a different origin
questions.why: Users trust the domain in the link, then land on a lookalike login page. Allow only relative paths (starting with `/` but not `//`) or an allow-list of destinations. Cookies stay with your domain, but in OAuth flows an open redirect can leak authorization codes.
questions.asked: A classic review finding in login and logout flows.

questions.q: What does the `Strict-Transport-Security` header tell a browser?
choices: Encrypt the response body again on top of TLS, using the site's key
Reject certificates for the site not issued by one pinned authority
Use only HTTPS for this site for a set period, even if a link says http
Send every cookie over HTTPS only, even the ones without the Secure flag
questions.why: HSTS closes the gap where a first plain-HTTP request can be intercepted and downgraded before the redirect to HTTPS. Certificate pinning (HPKP) was a different, now abandoned header. The preload list covers even the very first visit.
questions.asked: A junior-level header question; the downgrade attack is the reason behind it.

questions.q: Your app prepends a 64-character pepper to each password before hashing it with bcrypt. What goes wrong?
choices: bcrypt rejects inputs over 64 bytes, so long passwords can no longer log in
The pepper makes every hash identical, because bcrypt then ignores the salt
The cost factor must be raised to match the longer input, or hashing times out
bcrypt uses only the first 72 bytes, so just 8 characters of a password count
questions.why: bcrypt silently truncates input at 72 bytes, so "pepper + password1" and "pepper + password9" hash identically. Apply a pepper as an HMAC over the hash, or use Argon2id. Tune the cost so one hash takes roughly 100 ms or more on your hardware, and raise it as hardware improves.
questions.asked: A production-experience signal: the 72-byte limit has caused real authentication bypasses.

questions.q: Why do many teams prefer progressive throttling to locking an account after five failed logins?
choices: Lockout only works with per-IP limits, which attackers dodge with proxies
Hard lockout lets anyone lock a victim out by failing their login on purpose
Lockout stores failed attempts, which counts as sensitive data under GDPR
Throttling stops credential stuffing completely, while a lockout never does at all
questions.why: Lockout turns your defence into a denial-of-service tool against specific users, and support pays for every unlock. Growing delays per account (plus per-IP limits, MFA and breached-password checks) slow attackers without handing them that lever. No single control stops stuffing completely.
questions.asked: A trade-off question: the strong answer names the abuse case of the obvious control.

questions.q: The rule is 'managers may approve expenses under £5,000 for their own team'. Why is plain role-based access control not enough?
choices: RBAC cannot represent a manager role, since roles only hold permissions
RBAC only covers read access, so approvals need a separate write model
RBAC checks run in the frontend, so the amount could be changed by users
Roles say what kind of user you are; the rule also depends on the data
questions.why: Being a manager is a role check; "under £5,000" and "their own team" are attributes of the expense and its owner. That needs policy- or attribute-based checks against the loaded resource (resource-based authorization in ASP.NET Core). Roles still do the coarse gate.
questions.asked: Real business rules rarely fit roles alone; checks you can model one.

questions.q: Which of these belongs in an audit log of login attempts?
choices: The submitted password on failures, so typos can be told from attacks
The session token issued on success, so admins can replay the session
Timestamp, account id, source IP, outcome and the reason for failure
The full request body, so investigators have every available detail
questions.why: You need who, when, from where and what happened to spot stuffing and investigate incidents. Passwords (even wrong ones are often a near-miss of the real one), tokens and raw bodies turn the log into a credential store that far more people can read.
questions.asked: Checks you log for investigation without creating a second breach.

questions.q: Why must a server verifying a JWT pin the expected algorithm rather than trust the `alg` value in the token's header?
choices: An attacker writes the header, so `alg` can say `none`, or `HS256` so your public key becomes the HMAC secret
Tokens signed with HS256 expire faster than RS256 ones, so the server must know which lifetime rule to apply
Libraries support one algorithm per key store, so a mismatched `alg` throws an error that leaks the key id
The `alg` header is encrypted with the signing key, so it cannot be read until the signature has been verified
questions.why: Verification must start from what the server expects (algorithm and key), never from the token's own claim about itself: `alg: none` asks for no check at all, and accepting HS256 where RS256 was issued lets an attacker sign with the widely known public key. Modern libraries reject `none` and take an allow-list; in ASP.NET Core that is `TokenValidationParameters.ValidAlgorithms`. The header is only base64url-encoded, and the algorithm says nothing about lifetime.
questions.asked: A classic JWT CVE class; a strong answer names both attacks and the library setting that closes them.

questions.q: What does a per-user salt add to a password hash?
choices: Identical passwords hash differently, so precomputed tables are useless
A second secret the attacker must steal before any hash can be cracked
Encryption of the hash, so a leaked table cannot be read without the key
A slower hash, since the algorithm runs once more for every salt byte
questions.why: With a unique random salt, two users with `hunter2` get different hashes, so a rainbow table or one crack covering many accounts stops working. The salt is not a secret and is stored beside the hash; the slowness comes from the work factor, not the salt.
questions.asked: Checks you know what salt is for; strong candidates add that it is not secret and not what makes hashing slow.

questions.q: A reviewer objects that bcrypt hashes in your users table contain the salt in plain text. How do you answer?
choices: They are right; the salt should move to a separate, access-controlled table
The salt is not secret; its job is uniqueness, and verify needs to read it
They are right; the salt should be encrypted with a key from the vault
The salt is only a hint for the library and is ignored during verification
questions.why: A bcrypt string such as `$2b$12$<22-char salt><hash>` carries algorithm, cost and salt so `compare` can recompute the hash. Hiding the salt adds nothing: its purpose is to make each hash unique, not to be unknown. A secret added to every hash is a pepper, which is a different thing.
questions.asked: Separates people who memorised 'salt your hashes' from people who know how a bcrypt string is laid out.

questions.q: For a new system in 2026, which password-hashing choice does the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet list first?
choices: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 1,000 iterations and a random 16-byte salt
SHA-512 applied 10,000 times in a loop with a per-user random salt
Argon2id with a minimum memory cost of about 19 MiB and a few iterations
AES-256-GCM encryption with a key held in the application's key vault
questions.why: OWASP recommends Argon2id first (memory-hard, so GPUs gain less), then scrypt, then bcrypt for legacy systems, with PBKDF2 at hundreds of thousands of iterations where FIPS compliance demands it. 1,000 PBKDF2 iterations is decades out of date, and encryption is reversible, which a password store must never be.
questions.asked: Asked to see whether your knowledge is current; naming Argon2id and why memory-hardness matters is the strong answer.

questions.q: How should a team choose the bcrypt cost factor for its login endpoint?
choices: Use the maximum the library allows, since a slower hash is always safer
Keep the library default forever, since changing it breaks old hashes
Pick 4, the minimum, and rely on rate limiting to slow attackers down
Tune it so one hash takes roughly a quarter of a second on your servers
questions.why: The cost is a trade-off: high enough to make offline guessing expensive, low enough that logins stay fast and cannot be used to exhaust CPU. Each hash stores its own cost, so raising it later does not break old hashes; they are upgraded on next login. Rate limiting does nothing once the table has leaked.
questions.asked: Shows whether you understand the work factor as a tunable cost, not a magic number.

questions.q: You raised your Argon2id memory cost. How do existing users' hashes get the new parameters without a forced reset?
choices: After a successful login, rehash the password just typed if its parameters are old
Run a migration that decodes every stored hash and re-encodes it with the new cost
Nothing is needed; the library applies new parameters to old hashes on verify
Email every user a reset link, since hashes cannot be changed without the password
questions.why: Only at login do you hold the plain password, so that is when you can rehash. Libraries expose a `needsRehash` check that compares the stored parameters with the current ones. Hashes are one-way, so no migration can re-encode them, and a mass reset punishes users for your configuration change.
questions.asked: A practical maintenance question; the strong answer says the parameters live in the hash string.

questions.q: You inherit 200,000 unsalted MD5 password hashes. What is the best way to protect them today, before users log in again?
choices: Leave them as they are and replace each one with Argon2id at the next login
Hash each MD5 value with Argon2id now; verify as Argon2id(MD5(password))
Encrypt the MD5 column with AES so a database dump no longer reveals them
Delete the column and let everyone use password reset to set a new password
questions.why: Wrapping the old hash in a slow hash protects every account immediately; at each login you can then compute `argon2id(md5(pw))`, and later rehash to plain Argon2id. Waiting for logins leaves dormant accounts crackable for years, and encryption only moves the problem to wherever the key lives.
questions.asked: A real legacy-code scenario; strong candidates think about dormant accounts, not only active ones.

questions.q: Which password rule does current NIST guidance (SP 800-63B) tell you to drop?
choices: A minimum length, since users choose longer passwords unprompted anyway
Checking new passwords against lists of breached and common passwords
Forced expiry every 90 days when there is no sign of any compromise
Allowing spaces and all printable Unicode characters in the password
questions.why: Scheduled rotation pushes users towards `Summer2026!` then `Autumn2026!`, so NIST says change only on evidence of compromise, and drop composition rules too. Minimum length and breached-password screening are what it keeps, and it explicitly allows spaces and Unicode.
questions.asked: Checks you follow current guidance rather than the rules on your bank's website.

questions.q: Why should a signup form not cap passwords at 16 characters?
choices: Long passwords make the hash slower, so the cap exists only for performance
The cap breaks bcrypt, which needs at least 20 bytes of input to be secure
The cap is fine as long as the form also demands a symbol and a digit
It blocks passphrases and generated passwords, the strongest kind
questions.why: Password managers and passphrases produce long secrets; a short cap forces weaker ones and hints that passwords may be stored rather than hashed. Allow at least 64 characters, but do set a sane upper bound (and remember bcrypt's 72-byte input limit) so huge inputs cannot be used to burn CPU.
questions.asked: A junior-friendly design question; mentioning password managers and an upper bound for DoS rounds it out.

questions.q: In this login handler, what can an attacker learn from response times alone?
choices: Which emails have accounts, since unknown emails skip the slow verify
The password length, since verify takes longer for longer passwords
Nothing, since both failure paths return the same status and message
The Argon2id parameters, since verify time grows with the memory cost
questions.why: Unknown emails return in a millisecond; known ones take the hash time, so the identical message still leaks account existence. Verify against a fixed dummy hash when the user is missing so both paths do the same work. Argon2 time does not depend on password length in any useful way.
questions.asked: Follows up the 'same error message' answer to see whether you think about side channels.

questions.q: What is credential stuffing?
choices: Guessing many common passwords against one account until one works
Replaying username and password pairs leaked from other sites
Injecting extra fields into a login form to bypass validation
Stealing session cookies and replaying them from another device
questions.why: People reuse passwords, so pairs from one breach unlock accounts elsewhere. It succeeds with very few attempts per account, so per-account lockout barely touches it; MFA, breached-password checks and bot detection do. Many guesses against one account is brute force.
questions.asked: The most common real attack on login forms; interviewers want the defences, not just the definition.

questions.q: How does password spraying differ from a brute-force attack on one account?
choices: Spraying guesses many passwords quickly against one known admin account
Spraying uses stolen hashes offline, while brute force hits the live form
Spraying tries a few common passwords across many accounts, slowly
Spraying needs a valid session first, while brute force starts with none
questions.why: One or two attempts per account stays below any per-account lockout threshold, and `Winter2026!` across 10,000 accounts will find someone. Detecting it needs global monitoring of failure rates and breached or common password bans. Offline cracking of leaked hashes is a separate threat.
questions.asked: Tests whether you see why per-account throttling alone is not enough.

questions.q: Which is the safest way to generate a password-reset token in Node 24?
choices: Math.random().toString(36).slice(2), repeated until it is 32 characters
A SHA-256 hash of the user's email concatenated with Date.now()
A UUID v1, since it combines the time with the server's MAC address
crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'), from the OS's CSPRNG
questions.why: `randomBytes` draws from a cryptographically secure generator, giving 256 unguessable bits. `Math.random` is predictable once enough outputs are seen, a hash of email plus time can be brute-forced over a small time window, and UUID v1 is built from guessable time and machine data.
questions.asked: Checks you know Math.random is not for secrets; naming the CSPRNG and bit length is the strong answer.

questions.q: A user submits 'Forgot password' with an email. What should the response say?
choices: The same message either way, such as 'If that account exists, we sent a link'
'No account with that email' when missing, so the user can try another address
A 404 for unknown emails and a 202 for known ones, following REST conventions
The masked email of the matching account, so users can see which one they used
questions.why: Reset endpoints are a favourite enumeration oracle: an attacker checks which emails have accounts before stuffing credentials. Send the same response and roughly the same timing either way, and email the address itself. Signup has the same problem; handle it by emailing 'you already have an account'.
questions.asked: Asked to see if you apply enumeration thinking beyond the login form.

questions.q: Why store only a hash of each password-reset token rather than the token itself?
choices: Hashing makes the token shorter, so it fits in an email link safely
A read-only database leak would hand out working reset links
Hashing lets the server recover the user id without a database lookup
Email providers reject links whose tokens appear in plain text logs
questions.why: A valid reset token is as good as a password for its lifetime, so treat it like one. Because the token is random and high-entropy, a fast SHA-256 is enough; no salt or slow hash is needed. You look up the row by the token's hash when the link is followed.
questions.asked: A strong answer also explains why a fast hash is fine here but not for passwords.

questions.q: Your reset email builds its link from the request. What is the vulnerability?
questions.code:
const link = `https://${req.headers.host}/reset?token=${token}`;
await mailer.send(user.email, `Reset your password: ${link}`);
choices: The token is placed in a query string, which email clients refuse to open
The link uses HTTPS, which breaks when the app runs behind a load balancer
An attacker sets Host to their domain, so the link leaks the token
Template literals do not escape the token, allowing script in the email
questions.why: Host header poisoning: the attacker requests a reset for the victim with `Host: evil.example`, and the genuine email points at the attacker's server, which receives the token when the victim clicks. Build links from a configured base URL, never from request headers.
questions.asked: A known real-world bug class; good candidates generalise to 'never trust Host for absolute URLs'.

questions.q: The reset page at `/reset?token=…` loads an analytics script and links to your help site. How can the token leak, and what reduces it?
choices: Through the browser cache; send `Cache-Control: public` on the reset page
Through the page title; set a generic `<title>` that omits the token
Through cookies; mark the reset page's cookies `SameSite=Strict`
Through the Referer header; set `Referrer-Policy` and swap the token quickly
questions.why: Third-party scripts can read the URL, and requests from the page can send it in `Referer`. Set `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` (or `strict-origin`), keep third-party scripts off the page, and exchange the token for a short-lived server session on first load so the URL is dead afterwards. `public` caching would make it worse.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think about where URLs travel; most candidates forget analytics scripts.

questions.q: Why are 'security questions' like 'What was your first pet's name?' a weak recovery method?
choices: The answers are often guessable or findable on social media
The answers must be stored in plain text so they can be compared
They cannot be used without SMS, so they inherit SIM-swap risk
They violate WCAG, since the questions cannot be read aloud
questions.why: Answers are low-entropy, public or shared with family, and users cannot change their first pet. NIST no longer allows them. The answers can be hashed like passwords, so plain storage is not the real flaw.
questions.asked: Quick check that you know which recovery methods are considered broken.

questions.q: What is the main risk of SMS as the account-recovery channel?
choices: SMS messages are too short to hold a secure one-time code
SIM swapping lets an attacker receive the victim's texts
Phones cache SMS codes forever, so they can be replayed
Carriers forward every SMS to a public logging service
questions.why: An attacker who talks a carrier into porting the number gets every code sent to it, and has thus taken over any account that recovers by SMS alone. SMS is still better than nothing as a second factor, but recovery should prefer email, backup codes or a second passkey.
questions.asked: Checks you know the concrete attack; strong answers propose recovery codes or passkeys instead.

questions.q: A signed-in user asks to change their account email. Which flow is safest?
choices: Update the address immediately, since the user is already authenticated
Update it, then send a confirmation link to the new address afterwards
Re-authenticate, confirm via the new address, and notify the old one
Require the user to contact support, since email changes are too risky
questions.why: Email is the recovery channel, so changing it is a takeover step: a stolen session should not be enough. Ask for the password or a passkey, apply the change only after the new address confirms, and tell the old address with a way to undo it. Changing first means a typo locks the user out.
questions.asked: A design question about protecting the recovery channel; the notification to the old address is what strong answers include.

questions.q: Why do sites ask for your current password again before changing the password or deleting the account?
choices: It lets the server compare old and new hashes to block reuse
It refreshes the CSRF token, which expires when settings open
It confirms the password hash still uses the latest parameters
It stops someone with a stolen or unattended session doing damage
questions.why: Re-authentication (step-up) limits what a hijacked session or an unlocked laptop can do to the most sensitive actions. It also defeats CSRF on those endpoints as a side effect, but that is not the reason. Many apps also re-prompt for MFA or a passkey here.
questions.asked: A simple but telling question: good answers say 'step-up authentication' and name the threat.

questions.q: What does the `HttpOnly` cookie attribute do?
choices: Stops page JavaScript from reading the cookie through document.cookie
Sends the cookie only over plain HTTP, never over HTTPS connections
Sends the cookie only on HTTP requests, never over WebSocket upgrades
Marks the cookie as readable only by server-rendered HTML templates
questions.why: An XSS payload cannot exfiltrate an HttpOnly session cookie, though it can still make requests that carry it while it runs. HTTPS-only delivery is the `Secure` attribute; the name 'HttpOnly' means 'HTTP APIs only, not script'.
questions.asked: A warm-up; the strong follow-up is 'and what HttpOnly does not stop'.

questions.q: A session cookie lacks the `Secure` attribute, and every page redirects HTTP to HTTPS. What can still go wrong?
choices: Nothing, because the redirect happens before any cookie is ever sent
The first plain-HTTP request carries the cookie, exposing it on the network
JavaScript on the page can read the cookie, since Secure implies HttpOnly
The cookie is dropped after the redirect, so users are logged out at once
questions.why: A user typing `example.com` or following an `http://` link sends cookies before the redirect arrives; on hostile Wi-Fi that leaks the session. Set `Secure` and HSTS. Secure and HttpOnly are independent attributes.
questions.asked: Checks you understand the redirect is too late; mentioning HSTS preload is a bonus.

questions.q: What does the `__Host-` cookie name prefix guarantee in modern browsers?
choices: The cookie is encrypted with a key that only the host server knows
The cookie is hidden from JavaScript without setting HttpOnly separately
It was set Secure, with Path=/ and no Domain, so subdomains cannot set it
It is sent only to the host in the address bar, never to embedded frames
questions.why: Browsers reject a `__Host-` cookie unless it is Secure, has `Path=/` and has no `Domain`, so it is locked to one origin's host. That stops a compromised or careless subdomain from planting or overwriting your session or CSRF cookie (cookie tossing). It does not imply HttpOnly.
questions.asked: A deeper cookie question; strong candidates mention cookie tossing from subdomains.

questions.q: Your login sets the session cookie with `Domain=example.com`. What does that change?
choices: Nothing, since a cookie is always sent only to the host that set it
The cookie is blocked on example.com itself and sent only to subdomains
The cookie becomes a third-party cookie and is blocked by most browsers
Every subdomain, including a forum or marketing site, receives the session
questions.why: Setting `Domain` widens scope to all subdomains; leaving it out is what makes a cookie host-only. If `blog.example.com` runs third-party code or gets taken over, it receives your users' sessions. Only set Domain when you truly need cross-subdomain login.
questions.asked: Checks you know the counter-intuitive default: no Domain is the narrow option.

questions.q: Which pair of timeouts do session guidelines recommend for a typical business web app?
choices: An idle timeout after inactivity plus an absolute lifetime cap
An idle timeout only, since active users should never be logged out
An absolute timeout only, since tracking inactivity needs extra writes
No timeouts, relying on the user to click Log out when they are finished
questions.why: The idle timeout limits the window on an abandoned machine; the absolute timeout bounds how long a stolen session keeps working even when the attacker keeps it busy. The values depend on risk: minutes for banking, hours or days for low-risk apps.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can explain what each timeout defends against.

questions.q: What must a logout endpoint do when you use server-side sessions?
choices: Clear the cookie in the browser; the server copy expires on its own later
Delete or invalidate the session on the server, then clear the cookie
Redirect to the home page with Cache-Control: no-store on the response
Rotate the session id, keeping the same session data for the next login
questions.why: If only the cookie is cleared, anyone who copied the session id can keep using it until it expires. `req.session.destroy()` in express-session or `SignOutAsync` removing the server ticket is the real logout. Rotating the id is what happens on login, not logout.
questions.asked: A basic correctness check; strong answers contrast it with the difficulty of logging out a JWT.

questions.q: How much randomness should a session id have, according to OWASP?
choices: Enough to be unique, so an auto-increment integer is acceptable
At least 8 bits, provided the id is also signed with an HMAC
At least 64 bits of entropy, from a secure random source
Exactly 128 characters, since shorter ids are always guessable
questions.why: An id with 64 or more bits of CSPRNG entropy cannot be guessed even across millions of live sessions. Uniqueness is not enough, because a predictable id is a session hijack. Length in characters says little; entropy is what counts.
questions.asked: Checks you distinguish unique from unguessable; frameworks do this for you, but you should know why.

questions.q: You store the whole session in a signed cookie (for example `cookie-session`). What is the security trade-off compared with a server-side store?
choices: The browser can edit the data freely, since signing only hides it
The cookie becomes readable by JavaScript even with HttpOnly set
Signing needs a database round trip, so every request is slower
The server cannot revoke it; a copied cookie works until it expires
questions.why: A signed cookie is a stateless token with the same trade-off as a JWT: tampering is detected, but logout only asks the browser to forget it. Keep lifetimes short or add a server-side version check. Signing prevents edits but does not hide the data unless it is also encrypted.
questions.asked: Tests whether you recognise a cookie session as a stateless token in disguise.

questions.q: What is the safest way to implement 'Remember me for 30 days'?
choices: A separate random token, stored hashed and rotated each time it is used
Store the user's email and password hash in a long-lived cookie
Extend the normal session cookie's Max-Age to 30 days, unchanged
Keep the user's id in localStorage and log them in from it on load
questions.why: A dedicated long-lived token can be revoked, rotated on each use so theft is detectable, and exchanged for a fresh short session. A 30-day main session widens the hijack window for everything, and a stored user id is not a credential at all.
questions.asked: A design question; strong candidates mention rotation and requiring re-auth for sensitive actions.

questions.q: A cookie is set with no `Expires` or `Max-Age`. How long does it live?
choices: Exactly 24 hours, which is the browser default for any cookie
Until the browser session ends, though session restore may keep it
Forever, until the server explicitly sends a deleting cookie back
Only for the current page load, and it is gone on the next navigation
questions.why: A session cookie is dropped when the browser session ends, but modern browsers that restore tabs often restore session cookies too, so do not rely on it for logout. The server-side idle and absolute timeouts are what actually bound the session.
questions.asked: A quick fact check with a practical twist about session restore.

questions.q: Why does OWASP advise against blocking paste in password fields?
choices: Blocking paste breaks screen readers, which paste text in the background
Pasted passwords are sent in plain text, so blocking paste changes nothing
It pushes users away from password managers towards short typed passwords
Browsers ignore the block, so the code only adds maintenance for no gain
questions.why: Users with managers paste long random passwords; blocking paste makes them pick something typeable and memorable. The attack it imagines, a malicious clipboard, is not stopped by it anyway. NIST also says verifiers should allow paste.
questions.asked: A security-meets-UX question; it shows whether you think about user behaviour.

questions.q: How does the Have I Been Pwned range API let you check a password against breaches without sending it?
choices: You send the password encrypted with the API's public key over TLS
You send a bcrypt hash, which the service compares against its own table
You download the full breach list nightly and search it on your server
You send the first 5 hex chars of its SHA-1 and match the suffixes locally
questions.why: k-anonymity: the service returns every breached hash suffix sharing that prefix, a few hundred of them, and you compare locally, so the full hash never leaves your server. A bcrypt hash would be salted and uncomparable, and the full list is tens of gigabytes.
questions.asked: Shows you can implement 'block breached passwords' without creating a new leak.

questions.q: After a password reset completes, which follow-up matters most?
choices: End the user's other sessions and email them that the password changed
Keep the reset token valid for a day in case the user needs it again
Log the new password's length so support can help if the user forgets
Redirect to the login page with the email pre-filled in the query string
questions.why: A reset often follows a compromise, so existing sessions (including the attacker's) should die, and the notification lets a real owner react if the reset was not theirs. The token must be single-use; logging anything about the password leaks information.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think past the happy path to the account-takeover case.

questions.q: What is a pepper, as distinct from a salt?
choices: A second salt stored in the users table next to the first one
A secret added to every hash and kept outside the database
A random delay added to login responses to hide timing leaks
A per-user secret that the user must type in addition to a password
questions.why: A pepper is one application-wide secret (often an HMAC key in a vault or HSM), so a database-only leak does not give an attacker everything needed to crack hashes. Unlike a salt it must stay secret, and rotating it is hard, which is why it is optional.
questions.asked: Checks you can tell the two apart; strong candidates mention where the pepper lives.

questions.q: Why should a password-reset link expire within about an hour and stop working once used?
choices: Email servers delete messages that contain links after an hour anyway
The token's hash changes every hour, so older links cannot be matched
Old reset emails sit in inboxes and backups where others find them
It stops users from resetting too often, which fills the database
questions.why: An inbox compromised months later, a forwarded email or a shared computer should not yield a working takeover link. Short expiry and single use bound that exposure. Also invalidate outstanding tokens when the password changes by any route.
questions.asked: A junior-level question that tests whether you think about where emails end up.

questions.q: Which is the strongest self-service recovery option to offer users who enabled MFA and lost their phone?
choices: An SMS code sent to the phone number on the account
A security question chosen when the user enabled MFA
Resetting MFA by email with no further check at all
One-time backup codes issued and saved at enrolment
questions.why: Backup codes are offline, single-use and were saved while the user was known to be genuine. If losing the device lets email alone disable MFA, MFA only protects against attackers without email access. A second registered passkey is equally good.
questions.asked: Recovery is where MFA is weakest; interviewers want to hear you close the loophole.

questions.q: What problem does the `SameSite=Lax` default in modern browsers not solve?
choices: State-changing GET endpoints, which Lax still sends on cross-site links
Cross-site form POSTs, which Lax still sends with the session cookie
Cross-site image requests, which Lax still sends with the session cookie
Cross-site fetch calls, which Lax still sends when credentials are included
questions.why: Lax sends cookies on top-level GET navigations, so `GET /account/delete` triggered from a link on another site still arrives authenticated. Lax does withhold cookies from cross-site POSTs, images and fetch calls. The fix is never to change state on GET.
questions.asked: A follow-up to 'what is SameSite'; it checks you know exactly what Lax allows.

questions.q: Your app offers 'Sign in with Google'. In OAuth terms, which party is the authorization server?
choices: Your backend, because it decides which users may use your app
The user's browser, because it carries the redirect between sites
Your React app, because it starts the flow and receives the code
Google, because it authenticates the user and issues the tokens
questions.why: Google's identity service logs the user in and issues codes and tokens; your app is the client (relying party in OIDC terms), and the user is the resource owner. An API that accepts Google's access tokens would be the resource server. Getting the roles straight makes every other OAuth question easier.
questions.asked: A vocabulary check that sets up harder OAuth questions; get the four roles right.

questions.q: What does the `state` parameter in an OAuth authorization request protect against?
choices: An attacker completing a login flow in your browser with their code
An attacker reading the access token from the redirect URL's fragment
An attacker replaying a stolen ID token against another application
An attacker swapping the client_id for one registered to their own app
questions.why: `state` is a random value tied to the user's browser session and checked on the callback, so a callback the user never started is rejected. Without it an attacker can feed you their own authorization code and log you into their account (login CSRF). PKCE also covers code injection; replayed ID tokens are what `nonce` addresses.
questions.asked: Checks you know why the callback needs its own CSRF protection.

questions.q: In OpenID Connect, what is the `nonce` parameter for?
choices: It encrypts the ID token so only the requesting client can read it
It binds the ID token to this login request, so old ones cannot be replayed
It rate-limits the authorization server's token endpoint per client
It tells the provider how long the user's session should stay valid
questions.why: The client sends a random nonce, the provider copies it into the ID token, and the client checks they match, so an ID token captured from another flow is rejected. It is the ID-token counterpart of `state`, which protects the callback request itself.
questions.asked: Often asked straight after `state`; the strong answer contrasts the two.

questions.q: Why must an authorization server match the `redirect_uri` exactly against the registered list, rather than by prefix or wildcard?
choices: Prefix matching is slower, and the token endpoint must answer quickly
Browsers refuse redirects to any URL that has query string parameters
A loose match lets an attacker send codes to a page or host they control
Exact matching lets the server derive the client secret from the URL
questions.why: If `https://app.example.com/*` is allowed, an open redirect or user-controlled page anywhere under it can receive the authorization code or token. OAuth 2.1 and the security BCP require exact string matching. As a client, register only the precise callback URLs you use.
questions.asked: Tests whether you connect OAuth redirect rules to open-redirect bugs.

questions.q: What is the status of the OAuth implicit flow in current guidance (OAuth 2.1 and the security BCP)?
choices: It is recommended for SPAs, since they cannot keep a client secret
It is allowed only when the SPA also uses a refresh token rotation
It is recommended for mobile apps and deprecated for web apps only
It is removed; use the authorization code flow with PKCE instead
questions.why: Implicit returned the access token in the URL fragment, where history, logs, extensions and injected scripts could reach it, with no way to bind it to the client. Browsers now support the code flow with PKCE via CORS, so implicit has no remaining use.
questions.asked: Checks your OAuth knowledge is current; many tutorials still show implicit.

questions.q: What is the backend-for-frontend (BFF) pattern for SPA authentication?
choices: A server-side component runs the OAuth flow and keeps the tokens; the browser gets a cookie
The SPA stores tokens in localStorage and a backend refreshes them on a timer
The SPA sends the user's password to a backend, which exchanges it for tokens
Each microservice runs its own login page, so the SPA never handles tokens
questions.why: Tokens never reach JavaScript, so XSS cannot steal them; the SPA talks to its BFF with an HttpOnly, SameSite session cookie, and the BFF attaches access tokens to upstream API calls. It is the current IETF recommendation for browser apps, at the cost of running a server and handling CSRF.
questions.asked: Senior-leaning; strong candidates explain what it protects against and what it costs.

questions.q: When a user signs in with an OIDC provider, which claim pair should your users table use as the stable key for that identity?
choices: `email`, since it is unique per person and users recognise it
`iss` plus `sub`, since `sub` is unique and stable per issuer
`name` plus `email`, since together they are hard to collide
`aud` plus `sub`, since `aud` names your application's client
questions.why: `sub` never changes for a user at that issuer, whereas emails change and can be reassigned; keying on email lets a new owner of an old address inherit an account. `sub` is only unique within an issuer, so store it with `iss` if you support several providers.
questions.asked: A data-modelling question disguised as auth; it catches the 'we key on email' bug.

questions.q: You add 'Sign in with Microsoft' next to 'Sign in with Google' and auto-link accounts that share an email. What must you check?
choices: That both providers return the same `sub`, which proves one person
That the ID token uses RS256, since only RS256 includes the email
That `email_verified` is true for a provider you trust to verify it
That the email domain matches your company's domain, and nothing more
questions.why: If a provider lets users claim unverified emails, an attacker registers the victim's address there and gets linked straight into the victim's account. Only link on verified emails from providers you trust, or ask the user to sign in with the existing method first. `sub` values differ across providers by design.
questions.asked: A real account-takeover class; interviewers like candidates who question auto-linking.

questions.q: Which scope must an OAuth request include for the provider to return an OpenID Connect ID token?
choices: `profile`, since the ID token exists to carry the user's profile
`offline_access`, since ID tokens are issued with refresh tokens
`email`, since an ID token without an email would be meaningless
`openid`, which is what turns the request into an OIDC request
questions.why: Without `openid` it is plain OAuth and you get only an access token. `profile` and `email` add claims, and `offline_access` asks for a refresh token; neither creates an ID token on its own.
questions.asked: A practical detail you hit the first time you configure an OIDC client.

questions.q: A user clicks Log out in your app, which uses OIDC with a corporate identity provider. Clicking 'Sign in' again logs them straight back in without a prompt. Why?
choices: Your app cleared its session but the provider's session is still alive
The ID token was cached by the browser and reused on the next request
The refresh token was not revoked, so the SPA silently renewed its tokens
The provider ignores logout for users who ticked 'Stay signed in'
questions.why: There are two sessions: yours and the provider's single sign-on session. To end both, redirect to the provider's `end_session_endpoint` (RP-initiated logout) after clearing your own. Whether to do that is a product decision; on shared machines you usually should.
questions.asked: A support-ticket scenario; the strong answer names RP-initiated logout.

questions.q: Why does the authorization code flow return a short-lived code to the browser instead of the tokens themselves?
choices: Codes are shorter, so they fit into URLs that browsers can handle
The tokens are then fetched over a back channel, bound to the client
Codes are encrypted, whereas tokens are always sent as plain JSON
Browsers block redirects that carry anything that looks like a JWT
questions.why: The redirect passes through the browser, history and possibly logs, so it carries only a one-time code; the client redeems it directly with the token endpoint using its secret or PKCE verifier. An intercepted code alone is therefore useless, and it expires within seconds or minutes.
questions.asked: The core idea of the flow; explaining front channel versus back channel shows real understanding.

questions.q: Which pair of credentials gives true two-factor authentication?
choices: A password and the answer to a security question
A password and a PIN chosen at registration time
A password and a code from an authenticator app
A password and the user's date of birth on file
questions.why: Factors must be of different kinds: something you know, something you have, something you are. A password plus a PIN or security answer is two things you know, stolen by the same phishing page. The authenticator code proves possession of a device.
questions.asked: A basic definition check; strong candidates name the three factor categories.

questions.q: Why can a phishing site steal a TOTP code but not a passkey login?
choices: Passkeys use longer codes, which attackers cannot type fast enough
Passkeys are stored on a server, so there is nothing on the device to steal
TOTP codes are sent by SMS, which attackers can intercept in transit
The browser binds the passkey signature to the real site's origin
questions.why: A user can type a TOTP code into a look-alike site, which relays it within its 30-second window. With WebAuthn the browser includes the actual origin in what the authenticator signs, and the credential is scoped to your domain, so a look-alike domain gets nothing usable.
questions.asked: The single most important property of passkeys; interviewers want 'origin-bound'.

questions.q: What does your server store for each registered passkey?
choices: The credential id and the public key, plus a signature counter
The private key, encrypted with a key held in your secrets vault
A hash of the user's fingerprint, used to match future sign-ins
A shared secret, hashed with Argon2id like an ordinary password
questions.why: The private key never leaves the authenticator; the server verifies signatures with the public key, so a database leak reveals nothing that can log anyone in. Biometrics are checked locally by the device and never sent to you.
questions.asked: Checks you understand why a passkey database breach is harmless compared with a password one.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between a synced passkey and a device-bound one?
choices: Synced passkeys use passwords under the hood, so they are only one factor
Synced ones back up across a user's devices; device-bound ones stay on one key
Device-bound passkeys work on any site, while synced ones are tied to one
Synced passkeys cannot be used for login, only as a second factor after it
questions.why: Passkeys in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager or a password manager sync end-to-end encrypted, so losing a phone does not lock the user out. Hardware security keys keep the private key on the device, which suits high-assurance roles but needs a backup key. Both are origin-bound.
questions.asked: A 2026-relevant question; strong answers tie it to account recovery.

questions.q: In WebAuthn, why must the server generate a fresh random challenge for each sign-in and accept it only once?
choices: The challenge doubles as the session id after the ceremony succeeds
The authenticator uses it as the seed for a brand-new key pair
Otherwise a captured signed response could be replayed to log in
Browsers reject any challenge they have seen before from that site
questions.why: The authenticator signs the challenge, so a unique, single-use, short-lived challenge makes each signature valid for one ceremony only. Store it server-side (for example in the pre-login session) and delete it when verified. Libraries such as SimpleWebAuthn do the crypto but not your challenge storage.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand the challenge-response core rather than just calling a library.

questions.q: What does setting WebAuthn `userVerification: 'required'` mean?
choices: The server must email the user to confirm each new sign-in attempt
The browser sends the user's fingerprint image to the server to check
The user must also enter their password after using the passkey
The authenticator must confirm the user locally with a PIN or biometric
questions.why: User verification proves the person holding the device unlocked it, which makes the passkey alone multi-factor: possession of the device plus a PIN or biometric. The biometric data never leaves the device; the server only sees a UV flag in the signed data.
questions.asked: Explains why a passkey can replace password plus MFA; interviewers look for 'never leaves the device'.

questions.q: How should a server validate TOTP codes to stay usable but safe?
choices: Accept the current step and one either side, and reject a code once used
Accept codes from the last ten minutes, since phone clocks drift badly
Accept only the exact current step and no neighbours, however clocks drift
Accept any valid code at any time, since codes cannot be guessed anyway
questions.why: A small window absorbs clock drift and slow typists; remembering the last accepted step stops a code seen over someone's shoulder being replayed. Six digits is only a million options, so the MFA step itself also needs attempt limits.
questions.asked: Checks you know TOTP details beyond 'six digits every 30 seconds'.

questions.q: How should your database hold each user's TOTP secret?
choices: Hashed with Argon2id, the same way as the password
Encrypted at rest, since the server must read it
In plain text, since it is useless without the phone
Not at all; the authenticator app sends it at login
questions.why: The server computes the expected code from the secret, so it needs the raw value; a hash cannot be used. Encrypt it with a key outside the database so a dump alone cannot generate codes. The secret is exactly what the phone holds, so it is not useless to an attacker.
questions.asked: Tests whether you notice that TOTP secrets, unlike passwords, cannot be hashed.

questions.q: Attackers with a stolen password spam a user with push-approval prompts until they tap Approve. What mitigation do identity providers now use?
choices: Sending the prompt by SMS as well, so the user sees it twice
Lowering the push timeout so each prompt expires in five seconds
Number matching: the user types a number shown on the login screen
Letting users approve from a smartwatch, so prompts are harder to ignore
questions.why: MFA fatigue works because approving is one careless tap. Number matching means only the person looking at the real login screen can approve, and adds context such as location. Rate-limiting prompts helps too.
questions.asked: A real-incident question (it featured in well-known breaches); strong candidates name number matching.

questions.q: A passkey was registered with rpId `example.com`. Where can it be used?
choices: On any domain, since passkeys are tied to the user, not to a site
Only on the exact page URL where the passkey was first created
On example.com and example.net, since both share one company owner
On example.com and its subdomains, such as login.example.com
questions.why: The relying party id is a registrable domain the page's origin must equal or be a subdomain of, so `app.example.com` can use it but `example-login.com` cannot. That scoping is what makes passkeys phishing-resistant. Related Origin Requests exist for deliberate cross-domain use.
questions.asked: Checks you understand the scoping that underlies phishing resistance.

questions.q: Where do authorization checks have to run in a React app backed by an API?
choices: On the server for every request, whatever the UI shows or hides
In React route guards, since users cannot reach hidden pages
In the API gateway only, since services behind it are trusted
In the database only, since it is the last line of defence
questions.why: Anyone can call the API directly with curl, so hiding a button or guarding a route is only UX. Each endpoint must check the caller may perform this action on this resource. A gateway can do coarse checks, but the object-level decision needs the data the service loads.
questions.asked: The most basic authorization question; weak answers mention route guards.

questions.q: In a role-based access control design, why do teams check permissions like `invoices:approve` in code rather than role names like `Manager`?
choices: Permission strings are shorter, so JWTs carrying them are smaller
Roles can change what they grant without code edits everywhere
Frameworks such as ASP.NET Core cannot check role names at runtime
Checking permissions is faster, because roles need a database join
questions.why: `if (role === 'Manager' || role === 'Admin' || role === 'Finance')` spreads policy across the codebase; mapping roles to permissions in one place means adding a role or moving a permission is a data change. ASP.NET Core supports both; policies are its way of naming permissions.
questions.asked: A design question about keeping authorization maintainable as roles multiply.

questions.q: Which rule needs attribute-based access control (ABAC) rather than roles alone?
choices: Admins can delete any user account in the whole system
Support staff can view every open ticket in the queue
Staff may edit their department's documents in office hours
Guests can read the public price list on the website
questions.why: ABAC decides from attributes of the user (department), the resource (its department) and the context (time). The other rules are a role plus an action, which RBAC expresses directly. Most CRUD apps use RBAC for the coarse gate and a few attribute checks on top.
questions.asked: Checks you can tell when roles run out; strong answers mention combining the two.

questions.q: What is the most reliable way to enforce 'users can only read their own orders' in a SQL-backed API?
choices: Compare the order's email with the email the client sent in the query string
Switch order ids from integers to UUIDs so other users cannot guess them
Check in the React app that the order belongs to the signed-in user
Add `AND user_id = $2` with req.user.id, and return 404 when no row matches
questions.why: Scoping the query by the authenticated owner makes it impossible to fetch another user's row, even by mistake in a later refactor. UUIDs only make ids harder to guess, they leak in URLs and logs, and client-side checks are bypassed with curl.
questions.asked: The canonical BOLA fix; interviewers want it in the query, not bolted on after.

questions.q: A signed-in user requests `/documents/981`, which exists but belongs to another customer. Why do many APIs answer 404 rather than 403?
choices: 403 would confirm the document exists, leaking information to a prober
403 is reserved for users who are not authenticated at all
404 responses are cached by CDNs, so repeated probes are cheaper
The HTTP spec forbids 403 for requests that include a resource id
questions.why: Returning 404 for 'not yours' means the API reveals nothing about other tenants' ids. 403 is still right when the user may know the resource exists, such as a read-only member trying to edit a shared document. Unauthenticated requests get 401.
questions.asked: A subtle status-code choice; the strong answer gives a case for each.

questions.q: In a multi-tenant SaaS API, where should the tenant id used to filter queries come from?
choices: A `tenantId` field in the JSON body, validated to be a real tenant
The authenticated identity, such as a claim in the verified token
A custom `X-Tenant-Id` header that the React app sets on each call
The subdomain in the Host header, trusted without further checks
questions.why: Anything the client sends can be changed, so the tenant must come from the server-verified identity, or be checked against the tenants that identity belongs to. Subdomain routing is fine for picking a tenant, but must still be matched against the user's memberships.
questions.asked: Multi-tenant isolation is a frequent SaaS interview theme; this is its first rule.

questions.q: You enable Postgres row-level security on `invoices` with a tenant policy, but the app still sees every tenant's rows. What is the likely cause?
choices: RLS only applies to UPDATE and DELETE, never to SELECT statements
The policy needs an index on tenant_id before Postgres enforces it
The app connects as the table owner, and owners bypass RLS by default
RLS policies only take effect after the server has been restarted
questions.why: Table owners and superusers skip RLS unless you run `ALTER TABLE invoices FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, or better, connect as a non-owner role. RLS applies to SELECT too, and policies are live as soon as they are created.
questions.asked: A gotcha from teams adopting RLS; knowing it signals real Postgres experience.

questions.q: In ASP.NET Core, how do you check 'the user may edit this specific document' after loading it?
choices: Put `[Authorize(Roles = "Editor")]` on the controller and trust it
Read `User.Identity.Name` and compare it with the route's id value
Add a middleware that loads every document before routing happens
Call `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(User, doc, "CanEdit")`
questions.why: Resource-based authorization passes the loaded object to a policy's requirement handler, which can check ownership or attributes. The attribute runs before the document is loaded, so it can only check roles or claims. Comparing a name with a route id conflates two different things.
questions.asked: A .NET-specific question on putting ownership checks in a testable policy.

questions.q: In ASP.NET Core, what does setting an authorization `FallbackPolicy` that requires an authenticated user achieve?
choices: Endpoints without [Authorize] or [AllowAnonymous] require login by default
Users who fail a policy are redirected to a fallback error page instead
Anonymous users are allowed on every endpoint unless [Authorize] is set
The default policy is replaced, so [Authorize] now checks the admin role
questions.why: The fallback policy applies to endpoints with no authorization metadata, turning the app from default-allow into default-deny: a forgotten attribute becomes a 401, not a data leak. Public endpoints then opt out with `[AllowAnonymous]`.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know how to make 'deny by default' concrete in a real framework.

questions.q: Your API reads the user's roles from a 15-minute JWT. An admin is demoted at 10:00. What happens?
choices: The token is rejected at once, since the server re-reads roles on each call
Tokens issued before 10:00 keep granting admin until they expire
The refresh token is automatically revoked, logging the user out at 10:00
