The demotion is ignored until the user logs out, however long that takes
questions.why: Claims are a snapshot from issue time. Short lifetimes bound the window; for sensitive actions, re-check roles from the database or keep a per-user version that invalidates older tokens. The refresh token only helps if the refresh step re-reads roles.
questions.asked: Shows whether you understand the staleness cost of putting authorization data in tokens.

questions.q: A 'share this document with another user' feature makes access depend on relationships (owner, editor, viewer, member of a team with access). Which model fits best?
choices: Plain RBAC with a new role created for every document
An allow-list of IP addresses stored on each document
Relationship-based access control, as in Google Zanzibar
A per-document password that viewers must enter to open it
questions.why: ReBAC stores tuples like `doc:42#editor@user:7` and `doc:42#viewer@team:3#member`, then answers 'can user X edit doc 42' by walking relationships. Open-source systems such as OpenFGA and SpiceDB implement it. A role per document explodes the number of roles.
questions.asked: Asked where sharing features exist; naming ReBAC and a real tool is a strong signal.

questions.q: What does 'deny by default' mean for authorization code?
choices: Deny everything to new users until an admin approves their account
Return 403 for every request, then allow it on a retry with a token
Deny requests from unknown IP ranges before checking the user at all
If no rule explicitly grants access, the answer is no
questions.why: A missing check or an unmatched case should fail closed, so bugs cause errors rather than leaks. In code that means a `switch` over actions whose default denies, and in frameworks a fallback policy. It says nothing about account approval or IP ranges.
questions.asked: A principle question; strong candidates show how it looks in code.

questions.q: Your admin panel lives at `/admin-7f3a91`, a URL no one outside the team knows, with no auth check. What is wrong?
choices: Secret URLs leak via history, logs and Referer, so it is unprotected
The URL is fine, but the page needs a robots.txt entry to stay hidden
The URL is fine as long as it uses HTTPS, which encrypts the path
The URL should use a UUID instead, which is too long to guess
questions.why: Security by obscurity: the path ends up in browser history, proxy logs, analytics and Referer headers, and robots.txt publishes it to anyone who reads it. Every admin route needs an authenticated, authorised check; obscurity can only be an extra layer.
questions.asked: A quick test of whether you trust obscurity; robots.txt is the classic trap.

questions.q: Why should ownership filtering live in a shared repository method or query scope rather than in each controller action?
choices: Controllers cannot access the current user, only repositories can
One forgotten check in a new action becomes a data leak, so centralise it
Repositories run inside transactions, which authorization requires
Filtering in controllers is slower because it runs after serialisation
questions.why: Every new endpoint written by hand is a chance to forget `AND owner_id = ?`. Methods like `ordersFor(userId)` or EF Core global query filters by tenant make the safe path the default. Controllers can read the user fine; the point is removing repetition that can be forgotten.
questions.asked: A design question: interviewers want 'make the safe thing the default'.

questions.q: In EF Core, what is a common way to scope every query on `Order` to the current tenant automatically?
choices: An interceptor that rewrites every SQL string after it is generated
A database view per tenant, chosen by the connection string
A global query filter using a tenant id from a scoped service
A `[Tenant]` attribute on the entity that EF Core reads automatically
questions.why: `modelBuilder.Entity<Order>().HasQueryFilter(o => o.TenantId == _tenant.Id)` adds the predicate to every LINQ query on that entity. Remember `IgnoreQueryFilters()` exists, so review its uses carefully. There is no built-in `[Tenant]` attribute.
questions.asked: A concrete .NET technique for multi-tenant isolation; strong answers mention IgnoreQueryFilters.

questions.q: A support agent needs to see a customer's account to debug an issue. What is the safest way to build 'impersonation'?
choices: Give support staff the customer's password, reset after the call
Let support staff log in with an admin-only master password
Copy the customer's data into a support database each night
Issue a scoped, time-limited session recording both identities
questions.why: Impersonation should keep the real actor's identity in the session and audit log, restrict dangerous actions, expire quickly and ideally be visible to the customer. Shared or master passwords destroy accountability, and nightly copies spread personal data.
questions.asked: A realistic feature request; strong candidates talk about the audit trail.

questions.q: A comment containing a `<script>` tag is saved to the database and runs in every visitor's browser who views the post. Which kind of XSS is this?
choices: Reflected XSS, since the script is echoed back by the server
DOM-based XSS, since the script ends up inside the page's DOM
Stored XSS, since the payload is persisted and served to others
Self-XSS, since the attacker has to paste it into their own page
questions.why: Stored XSS is the most damaging kind because every viewer is hit without clicking a crafted link. Reflected XSS bounces a payload from the request (usually a URL) straight into the response; DOM-based XSS happens entirely in client-side code reading something like `location.hash`.
questions.asked: Vocabulary check; strong candidates add which one hits the most users.

questions.q:
In React 19, is rendering `

{comment.body}

` with attacker-controlled text an XSS risk?
choices: Yes, unless the text is passed through DOMPurify before rendering
Yes, because JSX compiles to innerHTML for text inside elements
Only in production builds, where React strips its escaping step
No, React inserts it as a text node, so markup is not interpreted
questions.why: JSX expressions become text content, so `<script>` shows up as literal characters. The dangerous paths in React are `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, URL-valued attributes such as `href`, and direct DOM access through refs. Sanitising already-safe text only mangles it.
questions.asked: Checks you know React's default protection and, in a follow-up, where it ends.

questions.q: Your CMS lets editors write rich HTML, which React renders with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. What makes this safe?
choices: Sanitise the HTML with an allow-list library such as DOMPurify
Escape the HTML with a function that replaces `<` and `>` first
Strip the word 'script' from the string before it is rendered
Rely on React, which blocks scripts in dangerouslySetInnerHTML
questions.why: When you need HTML, escaping would turn it into visible tags, so you sanitise instead: keep allowed tags and attributes, drop everything else, including `onerror` handlers and `javascript:` URLs. Deny-lists such as stripping 'script' miss ``. Browsers do not run inserted `
questions.asked: Tests whether you know the difference between escaping and sanitising.

questions.q: A profile page renders `Website`. Which stored value turns it into XSS, and what is the fix?
choices: `<script>alert(1)</script>`; escape angle brackets before rendering
`javascript:alert(1)`; accept only http and https URLs when saving
`https://evil.example`; block every domain that is not on an allow-list
`" onmouseover="alert(1)`; wrap the attribute value in single quotes
questions.why: A `javascript:` URL runs when clicked, and escaping HTML characters does nothing to it because the attribute holds a URL, not markup. Parse the URL and allow only `http:`/`https:` on input and output. JSX sets attributes as properties, so quote-breaking payloads do not apply; recent React versions warn about `javascript:` URLs, but do not rely on that.
questions.asked: The React XSS hole most candidates miss; interviewers look for 'validate the scheme'.

questions.q: In plain DOM code, which line is safe for displaying a user-supplied name?
choices: `el.innerHTML = name;`
`el.outerHTML = name;`
`el.textContent = name;`
`el.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', name);`
questions.why: `textContent` sets text, so any markup is shown literally. The other three parse their argument as HTML, where `` runs. Lint rules such as `no-unsanitized` flag the HTML-parsing APIs in review.
questions.asked: A fast filter question for anyone writing DOM code.

questions.q: Where should output encoding against XSS be applied?
choices: On input, once, by escaping all HTML before it is stored in the database
In the database, using a column type that escapes values automatically
In the CDN, which rewrites unsafe characters in every HTML response
On output, with the encoding for the context: HTML, attribute, URL or JS
questions.why: Only at output do you know the context, and each context needs different encoding: HTML-escaping is wrong inside a URL or a script. Escaping on input corrupts data for other consumers (emails, CSV, mobile apps) and double-escapes on display. Validate input, encode output.
questions.asked: A principle question; 'validate input, encode output' is the phrase interviewers want.

questions.q: A server template embeds initial state for the client like this. Why is it still an XSS risk?
choices: A string containing `</script>` closes the script block early
JSON.stringify runs user strings through eval before encoding
Browsers execute JSON keys that look like JavaScript functions
window properties can be read by scripts on any other origin
questions.why: The HTML parser ends the script at `</script>` before JavaScript sees anything, so a bio of `</script><script>alert(1)</script>` injects a new script. Serialise with a function that escapes `<` as `\u003c` (such as `serialize-javascript`), or put the JSON in a `<script type="application/json">` element and read it with `JSON.parse`.
questions.asked: A server-rendering gotcha; strong candidates know why JSON.stringify is not enough in HTML.

questions.q: What does this Content-Security-Policy do to an injected inline `<script>` without the nonce?
choices: It runs, because inline scripts are always allowed on the same origin
It is blocked, since only scripts carrying the per-response nonce run
It runs, but its network requests are blocked by the policy
It is blocked only in Chrome, since other browsers ignore nonces
questions.why: A nonce-based policy allows only scripts with this response's unguessable nonce, plus scripts they load (`strict-dynamic`). Injected markup cannot know the nonce, so it does not run. The nonce must be fresh on every response; a static one is worthless. All major browsers support it.
questions.asked: A strict CSP is Google's recommended XSS mitigation; explaining nonces shows depth.

questions.q: Your CSP is `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`. How much does it protect against XSS?
choices: Fully, since 'self' means only your own scripts can run on the page
Partly: it blocks inline scripts but still allows inline event handlers
Very little, since injected inline scripts and handlers are allowed
Fully, as long as you also set the X-XSS-Protection response header
questions.why: Most XSS payloads are inline, so `'unsafe-inline'` lets them run. Move to nonces or hashes to make CSP meaningful. `X-XSS-Protection` drove a now-removed browser filter; modern advice is to omit it or set it to 0.
questions.asked: Checks you can read a CSP rather than just knowing one exists.

questions.q: Your forum renders user posts written in Markdown. How can this still produce XSS?
choices: Markdown links always open in new tabs, which lets pages steal cookies
Markdown is compiled on the server, which runs any code in the post
Markdown headings are rendered as scripts in some older browsers
Most Markdown renderers pass raw HTML through unless configured not to
questions.why: The Markdown spec allows inline HTML, and link syntax accepts `javascript:` URLs, so the output needs sanitising or the renderer's HTML support switched off. Treat rendered Markdown like any other untrusted HTML.
questions.asked: A common real-world feature; interviewers check you do not assume Markdown is safe.

questions.q: Your session cookie is HttpOnly. Why is an XSS bug still serious?
choices: The script can act as the user from within the page as it runs
HttpOnly cookies can be read by scripts once the page has loaded
The script can switch off HttpOnly by setting the cookie again
It is not serious; HttpOnly makes XSS harmless for session apps
questions.why: Injected code runs with the page's origin, so it can call your API with the cookie attached, read what the user sees, change their email or show a fake login form. HttpOnly only stops the session being copied out for later use elsewhere.
questions.asked: Corrects the common belief that HttpOnly fixes XSS.

questions.q: Users can upload avatar images, served from your main domain. Why are SVG uploads a particular risk?
choices: SVGs are always larger than PNGs, so they fill the disk quickly
SVG is XML that can contain script, which runs when opened directly
SVG files carry EXIF metadata that includes the user's location
Browsers cache SVGs forever, so old avatars can never be replaced
questions.why: Opening `https://app.example.com/uploads/a.svg` renders it as a document on your origin, where embedded script can reach your cookies and API. Rasterise SVGs, serve uploads from a separate domain, or send `Content-Disposition: attachment` and a restrictive CSP.
questions.asked: Checks you think about uploads as content served from your origin.

questions.q: What does Trusted Types, enforced through CSP, add to XSS defence in Chromium-based browsers?
choices: It encrypts values written into the DOM so scripts cannot read them
It blocks all third-party scripts that are not listed in the policy
Sinks like innerHTML reject plain strings and need a policy-made value
It signs every response so the browser can detect injected markup
questions.why: With `require-trusted-types-for 'script'`, assigning a string to `innerHTML` or `eval`-like sinks throws; values must come from a named policy that sanitises them. That shrinks DOM XSS review from every sink to a few policies. It does not encrypt or sign anything.
questions.asked: Deep-dive territory; mentioning it shows you know modern DOM XSS defences.

questions.q: Which API is not exposed to classic CSRF?
choices: A form POST to an app that authenticates with a session cookie
A GET that changes state on an app using session cookies
A JSON POST to an app whose cookies have SameSite=None
A JSON API that only accepts a bearer token in Authorization
questions.why: CSRF works because the browser attaches cookies automatically; nothing attaches an `Authorization` header for another site. Cookie-authenticated endpoints, including JSON ones with `SameSite=None`, still need CSRF defences. Storing the bearer token in JS trades CSRF for XSS exposure.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand the root cause: ambient credentials.

questions.q: How does the synchronizer token pattern stop CSRF?
choices: The server issues a random per-session token and requires it in forms
The server checks that the session cookie matches the one sent at login
The browser adds a signed header to every form that another site submits
The server rejects any request that arrives without a Referer header
questions.why: An attacker's page can make the browser send your cookie, but cannot read your pages to learn the token, so its forged request lacks it. Frameworks do this for you: ASP.NET Core antiforgery, `csrf-csrf` in Express. Rejecting missing Referer breaks privacy-conscious users.
questions.asked: The classic defence; explain why the attacker cannot read the token.

questions.q: What is the weakness of a naive double-submit cookie (a random cookie value that must be echoed in a header)?
choices: Double-submit cookies are sent on every cross-site request by default
Anyone who can set cookies for your domain can plant a matching pair
The header is stripped by proxies, so real requests randomly fail
The random value must be stored server-side, defeating the point
questions.why: A subdomain or network attacker who can write a cookie on your domain sets both halves. Bind the token to the session with an HMAC (the signed double-submit pattern) and use a `__Host-` cookie. The pattern is stateless; that is its attraction.
questions.asked: Separates people who copied a pattern from people who know its assumptions.

questions.q: What does the `Sec-Fetch-Site` request header let a server do against CSRF?
choices: Read the attacker's origin, then block that origin in the firewall
Force the browser to resend the request with a CSRF token attached
Reject state-changing requests the browser marks as `cross-site`
Verify the session cookie's signature without a database lookup
questions.why: Fetch metadata headers are set by the browser and cannot be forged by page script, so a resource-isolation policy can refuse cross-site POSTs outright. It works in all modern browsers and is a solid extra layer, with CSRF tokens or SameSite as the baseline for old clients.
questions.asked: A modern defence few candidates know; mentioning it is a strong signal.

questions.q: A teammate says: 'Our cookie-authenticated API only takes JSON, so CSRF is impossible.' When is that true?
choices: Always, since browsers cannot send JSON from an HTML form
Always, since CORS stops the attacker's page making the request
Never, since JSON bodies are parsed before cookies are checked
Only if the server rejects any request not sent as application/json
questions.why: A form can send `text/plain` with a body that happens to be valid JSON, and CORS does not stop a simple cross-site request from being sent, only from being read. Requiring `Content-Type: application/json` forces a preflight, which blocks the forgery. Many body parsers accept anything by default.
questions.asked: A favourite follow-up; it tests your grasp of simple requests and preflight.

questions.q: What is login CSRF?
choices: An attacker signs the victim into the attacker's account without noticing
An attacker guesses the victim's password through a cross-site form
An attacker reads the login form's CSRF token from another origin
An attacker replays the victim's login request to renew the session
questions.why: The victim then saves card details or searches in an account the attacker can later read. Login forms need CSRF protection too, even though there is no session yet; that is why frameworks issue a pre-session token. OAuth `state` defends the same attack on social logins.
questions.asked: A lesser-known variant that shows you understand what CSRF really abuses.

questions.q: Which query is vulnerable to SQL injection?
choices: `db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', [email])`
`db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'")`
`db.users.findUnique({ where: { email } })`
`db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?', [email])`
questions.why: Concatenation puts user text into the SQL itself, so `' OR '1'='1` changes the query. Placeholders (`$1` in node-postgres, `?` in MySQL and SQLite drivers) send the value separately from the statement, and ORMs such as Prisma parameterise for you.
questions.asked: The entry-level injection question; any hesitation is a red flag.

questions.q: Your list endpoint accepts `?sort=created_at`. Why can't you pass `sort` as a query parameter placeholder, and what do you do instead?
choices: Placeholders only work for numbers, so cast the column name to an integer
Placeholders are slower, so build the whole query with template strings
Placeholders bind values, not identifiers; map input to allowed columns
Placeholders work fine for ORDER BY in Postgres, so nothing extra is needed
questions.why: `ORDER BY $1` sorts by a constant string, not a column, so dynamic identifiers must go into the SQL text. Only put in names from a fixed allow-list such as `{ created: 'created_at', name: 'name' }`; never echo the input. The same applies to sort direction and table names.
questions.asked: The practical exception to 'just parameterise'; very common in list-endpoint reviews.

questions.q: In EF Core 8+, which of these is vulnerable to SQL injection?
choices: `ctx.Users.FromSql($"SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Email = {email}")`
`ctx.Users.Where(u => u.Email == email).ToListAsync()`
`ctx.Users.FromSqlInterpolated($"SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Email = {email}")`
`ctx.Users.FromSqlRaw("SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Email = '" + email + "'")`
questions.why: `FromSql` and `FromSqlInterpolated` take a `FormattableString` and turn each `{}` hole into a DbParameter. `FromSqlRaw` takes a finished string, so concatenated input is part of the SQL. LINQ queries are always parameterised.
questions.asked: A .NET favourite; the strong answer explains FormattableString.

questions.q: What is the safe way to run an image tool on an uploaded file's name in Node?
choices: execFile('magick', [input, '-resize', '200x200', output])
exec(`magick ${input} -resize 200x200 ${output}`)
exec(`magick "${input}" -resize 200x200 "${output}"`)
spawn(`magick ${input} -resize 200x200 ${output}`, { shell: true })
questions.why: `execFile` and `spawn` without a shell pass arguments directly, so `; rm -rf ~` in a filename is just a strange filename. `exec` and `shell: true` hand the string to a shell, and quotes do not help because the input can contain quotes. Also prefix untrusted arguments or use `--` so names cannot become options.
questions.asked: Command injection in Node is common in upload and export features; this is the fix.

questions.q: A Node API passes the JSON body straight into a MongoDB query. What does this body achieve?
choices: Nothing, because MongoDB rejects operators inside query values
It logs in as the admin, since $ne matches any non-null password
It crashes the server, since the password field expects a string
It creates a new admin user with an empty password in the collection
questions.why: NoSQL injection: the operator object changes the query's meaning, much like `' OR 1=1`. Validate that fields are strings with a schema (Zod) or sanitise `$` keys. This code also shows a stored plain-text password, which is its own serious bug.
questions.asked: Checks you know injection is not only a SQL problem.

questions.q: What is second-order SQL injection?
choices: An injection that needs two separate HTTP requests in one session
An injection that only works against the database's second replica
Data stored safely is later concatenated into SQL by other code
A payload that is URL-encoded twice to slip past a web firewall
questions.why: A username like `x'; DROP TABLE…` is inserted with parameters, then a nightly report builds SQL from stored names. Data from your own database is still untrusted input. Parameterise every query, whatever the value's source.
questions.asked: Tests whether you treat your own database as a trust boundary.

questions.q: A download endpoint serves `path.join(UPLOAD_DIR, req.query.name)`. What input escapes the uploads folder, and what is the fix?
choices: `name=*.*`; reject any name containing a wildcard character
`name=%00`; strip null bytes, which end strings in Node
`name=CON`; block Windows reserved device names on input
`name=../../etc/passwd`; resolve the path and check its prefix
questions.why: Path traversal: `join` happily walks upwards. Resolve with `path.resolve` and confirm the result starts with the uploads directory plus a separator, or better, look files up by an id in the database and never use client-supplied names. Node rejects null bytes in paths.
questions.asked: A standard file-serving bug; strong answers suggest ids instead of names.

questions.q: What does this deep merge of a JSON request body allow?
choices: Every plain object in the process now has isAdmin set to true
Nothing, because JSON.parse drops any key named __proto__
A TypeError, because __proto__ cannot be assigned an object
Only the returned object gets isAdmin set to true
questions.why: `JSON.parse` creates an own key `__proto__`; the merge then reads `t.__proto__`, which is `Object.prototype`, and writes into it, so `({}).isAdmin` is true everywhere. Skip `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` keys, use `Object.create(null)` or `Map`, and validate bodies with a schema.
questions.asked: Prototype pollution is a Node-specific injection class; running through the mechanism impresses.

questions.q: In node-postgres, how do you safely filter by a list of ids from the client?
choices: `'WHERE id IN (' + ids.join(',') + ')'`, after checking the list is not empty
`'WHERE id IN ($1)', [ids.join(',')]`, sending one comma-separated string
`'WHERE id = ANY($1)', [ids]`, binding the whole array as one parameter
`'WHERE id IN ($1)', [ids]`, since pg expands arrays into a list itself
questions.why: Postgres accepts an array parameter, and `= ANY($1)` compares against each element, all safely bound. `IN ($1)` with a string compares id to the literal text `'1,2,3'`; `join` concatenation is injectable if ids are not validated numbers.
questions.asked: A daily CRUD need that trips people into concatenation.

questions.q: Is moving a query into a stored procedure enough to prevent SQL injection?
choices: Yes, because stored procedure parameters can never be treated as SQL
Yes, because the database compiles procedures before they receive input
No, since procedures cannot take parameters, so values are concatenated
No, if the procedure builds dynamic SQL by concatenating its parameters
questions.why: A procedure that does `EXEC('SELECT … WHERE name = ''' + @name + '''')` is injectable from inside. Use `sp_executesql` with parameters for dynamic SQL in SQL Server, or `EXECUTE … USING` in PL/pgSQL. The safety comes from parameters, not from where the code lives.
questions.asked: Catches the myth that stored procedures are inherently safe.

questions.q: An attacker submits a username containing a newline and the text `INFO login ok user=admin`. Your app writes `console.log('login failed user=' + username)`. What is the risk?
choices: Forged log lines that mislead investigators and log-based alerts
The server process crashes on the embedded newline character
The log file becomes executable, running the injected command
The newline is dropped, so the only risk is a slightly odd log
questions.why: Log injection lets attackers fake entries or hide their tracks. Structured JSON logging (Pino, Serilog) encodes values as fields, so a newline stays inside a string. Also keep secrets and personal data out of logs.
questions.asked: Links injection thinking to observability; strong answers propose structured logs.

questions.q: Which category sits at the top of the OWASP Top 10 for web applications in its recent editions?
choices: Injection, including SQL and command injection
Broken access control, such as missing ownership checks
Cross-site scripting in server-rendered templates
Security misconfiguration, such as default passwords
questions.why: Broken access control has been first since the 2021 edition, ahead of misconfiguration, supply-chain failures and cryptographic failures; injection (which now includes XSS) dropped from first place. It tops the list because it is found in most tested applications and no framework fixes it for you.
questions.asked: Checks awareness of the list and, more importantly, of why authorization bugs dominate.

questions.q: What does `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` prevent?
choices: Browsers caching responses that contain personal information
Other sites embedding your pages in a frame or an iframe
Browsers guessing a type and running an upload as script or HTML
Proxies compressing responses whose type they do not recognise
questions.why: Without it, a browser may sniff a file served as `text/plain` or an image and decide it is HTML or JavaScript, turning an upload into XSS. It costs nothing, so set it on every response; frameworks like Helmet do it by default. Framing is controlled by `frame-ancestors`.
questions.asked: A common security-header question; knowing what it blocks beats reciting its name.

questions.q: A developer says the API key in a config file is safe because it is Base64-encoded. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing, as long as the file is not committed to a public repository
Base64 is safe for keys, but it should be Base32 for URL safety
Base64 is a hash, so the app cannot recover the key to use it
Base64 is an encoding anyone can reverse; it is not encryption
questions.why: Encoding changes representation, encryption needs a key to reverse, and hashing cannot be reversed at all. A Base64 key is a plain-text key. Secrets belong in a secrets manager or environment injection, not in files.
questions.asked: A basic vocabulary check that exposes muddled thinking about crypto terms.

questions.q: Why is `eval(req.query.expr)` in a calculator endpoint so dangerous in Node?
choices: It runs arbitrary JavaScript with the server's full privileges
It is slow, so large expressions can block the event loop
It only accepts numbers, so any letter crashes the endpoint
It exposes the expression in logs, which leaks user input
questions.why: `require('child_process').execSync('…')` is a valid expression, so eval of user input is remote code execution. Parse the expression with a small grammar or a vetted library instead; `new Function` and `vm` without isolation are equally unsafe.
questions.asked: An easy one; hesitation here is a serious warning sign.

questions.q: Why should the whole site use HTTPS, not only the login and checkout pages?
choices: Search engines refuse to index any page served over plain HTTP
Session cookies and pages elsewhere can be read or altered in transit
HTTP pages load slower because they skip the browser's cache
Mixed sites break CORS, which blocks every API call from the app
questions.why: Every authenticated request carries the session cookie, and an attacker on the network can inject script into any HTTP page, including a fake login form. HTTPS everywhere plus HSTS closes both. Certificates are free, so there is no reason for exceptions.
questions.asked: A basic question that checks you know what TLS protects beyond passwords.

questions.q: A user can type text that your app later displays in an email subject line and in an HTML page. Where should you validate and where should you encode?
choices: Encode once when saving, since the value is then safe for any output
Validate on output and encode on input, so stored data stays safe
Validate the value on input; encode separately for each output context
Skip encoding, since validation removes every dangerous character
questions.why: Validation enforces what the value may be (length, allowed characters); encoding is output-specific, so the email subject needs header-safe handling and the page needs HTML escaping. Validation alone cannot strip everything dangerous in every context without mangling legitimate names like O'Brien.
questions.asked: Checks you can keep validation and encoding separate in your head.

questions.q: Your SPA sets `autocomplete="username webauthn"` on the email field. What does that enable?
choices: The browser stores the email in a cookie for the next visit
The browser skips the password field and submits the form at once
The email field becomes read-only once a passkey is registered
Passkey autofill, so saved passkeys appear in the field's suggestions
questions.why: This is WebAuthn conditional mediation: the page starts `navigator.credentials.get({ mediation: 'conditional' })` and the browser offers passkeys alongside saved passwords in the autofill menu, which makes passkeys discoverable without a separate button.
questions.asked: A practical passkey rollout detail; it shows you have built or read about a real flow.

questions.q: A developer pushed a `.env` file with the production database password to a shared GitHub repo, then deleted it in the next commit. What must happen first?
choices: Nothing more; the deleting commit removed the password from the repository
Rotate the password, since anyone may already have copied it
Rewrite the Git history to purge the file, then force-push the branch
Make the repository private so the old commit can no longer be viewed
questions.why: The secret is in history, clones, forks and possibly scrapers that watch GitHub for keys within seconds. Treat it as compromised: rotate, then check access logs. Rewriting history is worth doing afterwards, but it cannot un-leak a copied value.
questions.asked: A realistic incident question; the order of actions is what interviewers grade.

questions.q: A Vite React app reads `import.meta.env.VITE_STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` to call Stripe directly from the browser. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing, since Vite encrypts every VITE_ variable when it builds the bundle
Vite only exposes VITE_ variables in development, so production builds break
The value is inlined into the public bundle, so every visitor can read it
The variable must be named REACT_APP_ for Vite to load it at runtime
questions.why: Anything the browser needs is shipped to the browser. `VITE_` variables are replaced with their literal values at build time. Secret keys belong on a server, which calls Stripe on the client's behalf; only publishable keys go in frontend code.
questions.asked: The most common secret leak in React apps; interviewers want 'the bundle is public'.

questions.q: What does GitHub push protection for secret scanning do?
choices: Encrypts secrets in commits so that only repository admins can read them
Scans the repository's dependencies for known vulnerable package versions
Rotates any detected secret automatically with the issuing service
Blocks a push that contains a recognised credential before it lands
questions.why: Push protection checks commits for known token formats (cloud keys, Stripe keys, GitHub tokens) and rejects the push, which is far cheaper than rotating after the fact. Dependency scanning is Dependabot's job. Local pre-commit hooks such as gitleaks catch it even earlier.
questions.asked: Checks you know preventive tooling exists and where it sits.

questions.q: What does `npm audit` do?
choices: Compares installed package versions with a database of known advisories
Reads each package's source code to find new vulnerabilities in it
Removes any package that has not been updated in the last year
Verifies that each package was published by its original author
questions.why: It checks the resolved dependency tree against the GitHub Advisory Database and reports affected ranges. It knows nothing about undisclosed bugs, cannot tell whether your code reaches the vulnerable function, and does not verify publishers; that is what provenance and signatures address.
questions.asked: Basic tooling knowledge; strong answers mention its limits and noise.

questions.q: How does committing `package-lock.json` help supply-chain security?
choices: It encrypts dependencies so that attackers cannot read their source code
It pins exact versions and integrity hashes, so installs reproduce
It blocks packages with known vulnerabilities from ever being installed
It makes npm refuse packages that were published less than a week ago
questions.why: Without a lockfile, a `^1.2.0` range picks up whatever was published most recently, including a compromised patch release. The `integrity` field (a SHA-512 hash) means a tampered tarball fails to install. Lockfiles do not judge vulnerability; audits do.
questions.asked: A basic question; strong candidates mention the integrity hashes, not only version pinning.

questions.q: Why should CI install dependencies with `npm ci` rather than `npm install`?
choices: npm ci skips all lifecycle scripts, so no package code can run
npm ci downloads packages over a signed channel instead of HTTPS
npm ci installs exactly the lockfile and fails if it is out of sync
npm ci runs npm audit and stops the build on any known vulnerability
questions.why: `npm ci` deletes `node_modules`, installs precisely what the lockfile says and errors if `package.json` disagrees, so CI builds what you tested. `npm install` may update the lockfile. It still runs install scripts unless you add `--ignore-scripts`.
questions.asked: A practical CI question with a security angle.

questions.q: A teammate adds `reqeust` to package.json. Why is this worth stopping in review?
choices: npm rejects misspelled names, so the build will fail on the CI server
Misspelled packages are always older forks that lack security fixes
The package is valid, but npm will warn that its name is too short
It may be a typosquat: a malicious package named like a popular one
questions.why: Attackers publish packages with near-miss names that run a payload on install. Check new dependencies' names, publishers, download counts and repository links before adding them. Registries remove known squats, but new ones appear constantly.
questions.asked: Checks basic dependency hygiene; interviewers like 'I check what I add'.

questions.q: Why are npm `postinstall` scripts a supply-chain risk?
choices: They run arbitrary code on your machine or CI as soon as you install
They slow installs, which makes CI time out and skip security checks
They modify the lockfile, which hides the versions actually installed
They only run in production, so problems are missed during development
questions.why: Many real attacks (stealing tokens, planting backdoors) ran from install scripts before any of your code imported the package. pnpm 10 no longer runs dependencies' lifecycle scripts unless allow-listed, and npm supports `--ignore-scripts`. CI secrets should not be available during install.
questions.asked: Shows you know how compromised packages actually execute.

questions.q: What does a tool like Dependabot or Renovate do for a repository?
choices: Blocks every new release until a human has reviewed its source
Opens pull requests that bump dependencies, so tests check each update
Runs your production app in a sandbox to detect malicious behaviour
Replaces npm with a private registry that only hosts vetted packages
questions.why: Small, frequent updates through CI keep you close to patched versions, so a security fix is a one-line bump instead of a painful jump across majors. Grouping and scheduling rules stop the pull requests becoming noise.
questions.asked: Checks you have a routine for updates, not only for emergencies.

questions.q: Your page loads a library from a public CDN. What does adding an `integrity` attribute (Subresource Integrity) do?
choices: The browser downloads the file over an encrypted channel with the CDN
The CDN caches the file for longer, since its hash can never change
The browser refuses to run the file if its hash does not match
The script runs in an isolated sandbox with no access to the page
questions.why: If the CDN is compromised or serves a different file, the hash check fails and the script is blocked, which protects you from someone else's breach. It only works with pinned versions; `lib@latest` would break whenever it updates.
questions.asked: A concrete control against third-party script compromise.

questions.q: Why do security guides say to pin third-party GitHub Actions to a full commit SHA rather than a tag like `@v4`?
choices: Tags are case-sensitive, so a typo silently runs a different version
SHA pinning makes the workflow run faster because it skips resolution
GitHub deletes tags after a year, which breaks older workflows
Tags can be moved to a malicious commit; a SHA cannot be changed
questions.why: If an action's repository is compromised, the attacker can repoint `v4` and your workflow runs their code with your secrets, as happened in real incidents. A SHA is immutable; Dependabot can still update pinned SHAs for you. Also give `GITHUB_TOKEN` minimal permissions.
questions.asked: A CI supply-chain question drawn from real attacks; strong answers mention token permissions.

questions.q: Which of these should never be written to application logs?
choices: Bearer tokens and session ids from request headers
The request's HTTP method, path and response status
The authenticated user's internal numeric id
The duration of the request in milliseconds
questions.why: Logs are copied to many systems and read by many people, so a logged token is a credential leak. Configure redaction in your logger for `authorization`, cookies and password fields. Method, path, status, duration and user id are what you want for debugging.
questions.asked: A basic hygiene check; strong candidates mention automatic redaction.

questions.q: Your app must send customers' saved webhook signing secrets back to them later in the dashboard. How should you store them?
choices: Hashed with Argon2id, since secrets should never be stored reversibly
Encrypted with a key held outside the database, since you must read them
In plain text, because a webhook secret is not a user's password
Base64-encoded, which keeps them unreadable in the database dump
questions.why: Hash when you only need to verify (passwords, API keys you never show again); encrypt when you must recover the value. Keep the key in a KMS or vault so a database dump alone reveals nothing. Base64 is not protection.
questions.asked: Tests whether you pick hashing or encryption from the requirement.

questions.q: What does a valid TLS certificate for `shop.example.com` prove to the browser?
choices: The site is run by a trustworthy business that has been audited
The site's code has been scanned and contains no known malware
The server controls shop.example.com, as checked by a trusted CA
The site stores users' data encrypted on its own servers at rest
questions.why: Domain-validated certificates prove control of the name, and encryption plus that proof stop interception and impersonation. They say nothing about honesty: phishing sites have valid certificates too. The padlock is about the connection, not the company.
questions.asked: Checks you understand what HTTPS does and does not promise.

questions.q: What does the `exp` claim in a JWT mean?
choices: The time the token was issued, as seconds since the Unix epoch
The time after which the refresh token must be used to renew it
The number of times the token may be used before it is revoked
The time after which the token must be rejected, in epoch seconds
questions.why: `exp` is a NumericDate in seconds (not milliseconds, a common bug when comparing with `Date.now()`). Libraries check it for you, usually with a small clock-skew allowance. The issue time is `iat`; `nbf` is 'not before'.
questions.asked: A basic JWT claim; the seconds-versus-milliseconds detail impresses.

questions.q: Your company's API verifies JWTs in six services. Why sign them with RS256 or ES256 rather than HS256?
choices: Services verify with a public key and cannot mint tokens themselves
Asymmetric tokens are encrypted, so the claims are hidden from users
HS256 is deprecated in the JWT spec and rejected by current libraries
Asymmetric signatures are shorter, which keeps request headers small
questions.why: With HS256 every verifier holds the signing secret, so one compromised service can forge tokens for all of them. Asymmetric algorithms keep the private key at the issuer and publish public keys (JWKS). HS256 is still fine for a single app signing and verifying its own tokens.
questions.asked: Checks you understand symmetric versus asymmetric trust, not just algorithm names.

questions.q: A tutorial signs HS256 JWTs with the secret `secret123`. What can an attacker do with one captured token?
choices: Nothing, since the signature cannot be reversed to reveal the secret
Crack the secret offline, then forge tokens for any user they like
Read the payload, but only after decrypting it with the weak secret
Replay it once, since HS256 tokens are single-use by design
questions.why: The token contains the data and its HMAC, so an attacker can test billions of candidate secrets offline with tools like hashcat, then sign `{"sub":"admin"}`. Use at least 256 bits of random secret. The payload is readable anyway; it is only Base64url-encoded.
questions.asked: Demonstrates why secret strength matters for HMAC signatures.

questions.q: What does the word 'bearer' in `Authorization: Bearer <token>` imply?
choices: The token is bound to the device that first received it
The token must be accompanied by the user's password
Whoever holds the token can use it; nothing else is checked
The token is only valid for the request method it was issued for
questions.why: A bearer token is like cash: possession is authorisation, so a leaked one works from anywhere until it expires. That is why short lifetimes, TLS and careful storage matter. Sender-constrained tokens (DPoP, mTLS) exist to bind tokens to a key.
questions.asked: A vocabulary question with real consequences for token handling.

questions.q: An authorization helper throws an exception while loading the user's permissions. What should the request do?
choices: Allow it, since the user was already authenticated successfully
Allow it but log a warning so the team can investigate later
Retry the check up to three times, then allow it if it still fails
Deny it, returning an error rather than proceeding with the action
questions.why: Fail securely (fail closed): when a check cannot complete, treat the answer as no. A `try { check() } catch { /* ignore */ }` around authorization turns an outage in the permissions service into an open door.
questions.asked: A principle interviewers probe with a small code snippet; know the phrase 'fail closed'.

questions.q: How should an upload endpoint decide whether a file really is a PNG?
choices: Inspect the file's leading bytes and re-encode it with an image library
Trust the Content-Type header, since the browser sets it from the file
Check that the filename ends in .png before saving it to storage
Ask the user to confirm the file type in a dropdown on the form
questions.why: The extension and `Content-Type` are chosen by the client, so either can lie. Checking magic bytes is better, and re-encoding the image drops any appended payload and metadata. Still store uploads outside the web root under generated names.
questions.asked: Checks you know which parts of an upload request are attacker-controlled.

questions.q: You need to rotate the key that signs your session cookies without logging everyone out. What is the usual approach?
choices: Change the key at night, when few users are signed in to the app
Sign with the new key but accept either key for a transition period
Encrypt the old key with the new one and keep verifying with both
Stop signing cookies during the change and re-enable signing later
questions.why: Keep a key ring: new cookies use the new key, old ones still verify with the previous key until they expire, then remove it. `express-session` accepts an array of secrets for exactly this, and ASP.NET Core Data Protection manages a key ring automatically.
questions.asked: Rotation is routine operations work; interviewers want the overlap window.

questions.q: Your app runs in Azure or AWS and needs to read from a storage bucket. Why prefer a managed or workload identity over an access key in configuration?
choices: Managed identities are faster, since they skip the TLS handshake
Access keys cannot be used by .NET or Node SDKs any more
There is no long-lived secret to leak; the platform issues tokens
Managed identities give the app admin rights, so no errors occur
questions.why: The runtime obtains short-lived tokens for its own identity, so there is nothing to commit, copy or forget to rotate. Grant that identity only the permissions it needs. SDKs support both; the default credential chains try managed identity automatically.
questions.asked: The modern answer to 'where do you keep your cloud credentials'.

questions.q: What is the difference between encryption in transit and encryption at rest?
choices: In transit is for passwords and at rest is for every other kind of data
They are the same thing, applied by the database and the browser in turn
At rest protects data from users; in transit protects it from admins
In transit protects data on the network; at rest protects stored data
questions.why: TLS covers the wire; disk, database or field-level encryption covers stolen disks and backups. Neither protects against an attacker who compromises the running app, which sees plaintext. Interviewers often ask which your app has and why.
questions.asked: A basic distinction; strong answers note what neither protects against.

questions.q: A service encrypts card tokens in the database and keeps the encryption key in a column of the same database. What is the problem?
choices: Anyone with a database dump has both the data and the key
The key column slows every query that reads a card token
The database cannot store keys longer than 128 bits
Encryption keys must be rotated daily, which a column prevents
questions.why: Encryption only moves the problem to the key. Keep keys in a KMS, HSM or vault with separate access control, and ideally use envelope encryption so the KMS never hands out the master key.
questions.asked: Tests whether you see that key management is the real problem.

questions.q: What is a CVE?
choices: A certificate that proves a package passed a security review
A public identifier for a specific, disclosed vulnerability
A compliance standard that web applications must certify against
A scoring formula that rates how dangerous a vulnerability is
questions.why: A CVE id such as CVE-2024-12345 names one vulnerability so advisories, scanners and patches can refer to it. The severity score is CVSS, which is a separate thing and often overstates risk for your particular use.
questions.asked: Vocabulary you need to discuss scanner output; separating CVE and CVSS is a plus.

questions.q: Your site uses HTTPS everywhere. Which attack does that do nothing to stop?
choices: Someone on café Wi-Fi reading session cookies in transit
A proxy injecting ads or script into your pages on the way
SQL injection in a search box on your HTTPS site
An attacker impersonating your domain to steal passwords
questions.why: TLS protects the connection, and the payload is delivered faithfully, malicious or not. Injection, XSS and broken access control are application bugs that ride over HTTPS unchanged. Certificates and HSTS address impersonation.
questions.asked: Checks you do not treat HTTPS as a general security fix.

questions.q: Which is a classic 'security misconfiguration' finding in a production deployment?
choices: Using parameterised queries for every call from the ORM
Hashing passwords with Argon2id and a per-user salt
Setting session cookies as Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite
Running with debug mode on and a default admin password
questions.why: Debug pages leak stack traces and environment variables; default credentials are tried by every scanner. Misconfiguration also covers open storage buckets, verbose error pages and unnecessary services. The other options are correct configuration.
questions.asked: Checks you can give concrete examples of an OWASP category.

questions.q: A scanner finds `https://app.example.com/.git/config` returns your repository config. What is the risk?
choices: An attacker can download the repository, including history and secrets
The file only shows the remote URL, so there is no meaningful risk
Search engines will rank the site lower for exposing hidden files
The Git folder lets the attacker push commits to your repository
questions.why: With `.git` served, tools can reconstruct the source and every committed secret. It comes from deploying the working directory as the web root. Build artefacts should be deployed, and the web server should deny dotfiles. Pushing needs credentials the folder does not grant.
questions.asked: A realistic finding from a pentest; strong answers name the root cause.

questions.q: What does threat modelling ask about a feature before it is built?
choices: Which penetration testing firm should audit the feature once it ships
What can go wrong, who would do it, and what we will do about it
How many unit tests the feature needs to reach 80% code coverage
Which cloud region will host the feature so latency stays low
questions.why: A lightweight model sketches data flows and trust boundaries, then asks what could be spoofed, tampered with, leaked or abused (STRIDE is one checklist). Doing it at design time makes controls cheap. It is a team conversation, not a vendor engagement.
questions.asked: Asked at mid-level to see if you consider security before coding.

questions.q: What is an SBOM (software bill of materials) used for?
choices: Billing customers for each third-party library their tenant uses
Proving a package was built on a trusted CI server from its source
Listing every component and version in a build, to answer 'are we affected?'
Blocking any dependency whose licence is not on an approved list
questions.why: When a new vulnerability lands, an SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX) tells you within minutes which services ship the affected version. Provenance attestations are what prove where and how a package was built. Licence checks can use an SBOM but are not its purpose.
questions.asked: Increasingly required by customers; knowing what it answers is enough at mid-level.

questions.q: What does `npm publish --provenance` (npm provenance attestations) let consumers verify?
choices: That the package has no known vulnerabilities at publish time
That the package's licence allows commercial use in closed products
That the package author has enabled two-factor authentication
That the tarball was built from a given commit by a named CI workflow
questions.why: Provenance links the published package to its source repository and build via a signed Sigstore attestation, so a tarball uploaded from a stolen laptop token would lack it. `npm audit signatures` checks it. It says nothing about bugs or licences.
questions.asked: A 2026-current supply-chain control; mentioning it signals you follow the ecosystem.

questions.q: Your production site serves JavaScript source maps publicly. What is the main security consequence?
choices: Attackers can read your original frontend source, comments included
Source maps let attackers run code on the server that built them
Source maps expose server environment variables to every visitor
Browsers disable CSP on any page whose scripts have source maps
questions.why: Frontend code is public anyway, so this mostly makes reverse engineering easier, but maps also expose comments, internal URLs and occasionally hard-coded secrets. Many teams upload maps privately to their error tracker instead. They do not grant execution.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can weigh a finding's real severity rather than panic.

questions.q: Why is 'the admin page is only reachable from the office VPN' not a substitute for authentication on it?
choices: VPNs slow the page down, so users will find a way around it
Anyone on the network, or any compromised device on it, gets in
VPN traffic is not encrypted, so passwords would leak anyway
Admin pages must be public for search engines to index them
questions.why: Network location is a weak signal: laptops get malware, contractors join the VPN, and SSRF bugs let outside requests originate inside. Zero-trust thinking authenticates and authorises every request whatever its source. Network controls remain a useful extra layer.
questions.asked: A defence-in-depth question; 'zero trust' is the phrase to use.

questions.q: What is the security reason to keep third-party dependencies to a minimum?
choices: Every dependency makes the lockfile bigger, which npm cannot parse
Fewer dependencies mean fewer licences, which avoids any legal risk
Each one, plus its own dependencies, is code you run with full trust
Dependencies disable Node's permission model when they are loaded
questions.why: A package runs with your app's privileges, so a compromised `left-pad`-sized helper deep in the tree is a compromise of your app. Weigh a dependency's maintenance and reach against writing ten lines yourself. Licences are a separate concern.
questions.asked: Checks you think about the transitive tree, not only direct dependencies.

questions.q: A code reviewer finds `if (req.user.role = 'admin')` in an Express route. What does the bug do?
choices: Nothing, because JavaScript treats = and === the same inside if
It throws a TypeError, since role is a read-only property
It compares the strings but ignores differences in letter case
It assigns 'admin' and the check always passes for everyone
questions.why: Assignment returns the assigned value, and a non-empty string is truthy, so every caller becomes admin for the rest of the request. ESLint's `no-cond-assign` and TypeScript with strict linting catch it. It is a reminder that authorization code deserves tests of the 'deny' path.
questions.asked: A small review exercise; strong answers add 'test that non-admins get 403'.

questions.q: Why should authorization logic have tests for the deny path, not only the allow path?
choices: A check that always allows passes every allow test you write
Deny tests run faster, so they keep the CI pipeline quick
Frameworks only report coverage for code that returns 403
Allow-path tests are enough if the endpoint also has logging
questions.why: Most authorization bugs are missing or broken denials, and a happy-path test cannot see them. For every protected endpoint, test that another user, another tenant and an unauthenticated caller are refused. Table-driven tests keep this cheap.
questions.asked: Links security with testing; interviewers want 'test that other users are refused'.

questions.q: What is the point of an allow-list for input validation, compared with a deny-list?
choices: Allow-lists are faster, since they check fewer characters per value
Only known-good values pass, so forgotten bad patterns do not slip by
Deny-lists are illegal under data-protection rules in most regions
Allow-lists encode output automatically, which replaces escaping
questions.why: Attackers are better at finding the bad input you forgot than you are at listing it. Define what valid looks like (a schema, a set of sort columns, a URL scheme) and reject the rest. Validation still does not replace output encoding or parameterised queries.
questions.asked: A principle question; concrete examples make the answer strong.
